Combined with PTC1, the total series resistance from battery to VCC is bounded by 0.080 + 0.160 = 0.240 Ohm worst case, which at 480 mA is 55 mW, or 4.7% of the whole 1175 mW budget — that is why the input path is worth measuring with a milliohm meter before deciding anything here.
findings.risk: Weakens the last-ditch overcurrent protection from a 4.00 A to a 6.00 A five-second fusing current. Separate correctness note while I am here: F1 does NOT protect against a reversed battery pack. D1 (1SS355VMTE-17, cathode on BT1+, anode on GND per the board netlist) sits ACROSS the pack upstream of F1, so on reverse insertion the current loop is battery -> D1 -> battery and never passes through F1; the diode has to absorb the reversed pack's short-circuit current on its own until the cells sag or the user notices. That is a pre-existing upstream design property, not something the fork introduced, but it means F1's rating is only about downstream shorts and it is reasonable to trade some of it for resistance. Recommendation: measure first, and if you change anything, change PTC1 rather than F1 — the PTC gives more milliwatts per unit of protection given up.
findings.verify_reason: I fetched the Kyocera AVX Accu-Guard II datasheet and the table is exact: 'F0805B2R00FW/STR 2.00 0.080 220 4.00 0.030 63', 'F0805B2R50FW/STR 2.50 0.060 220 5.00 0.050 63', 'F0805B3R00FW/STR 3.00 0.050 220 6.00 0.10 63'. The column headers confirm the resistance is 'Resistance 10% x I rated, 25C, Ohm (max.)', the 220 mV is 'Voltage Drop @1 x I rated, 25C, mV (max.)' and 4.00 A is 'Fusing Current (within 5 sec), 25C'. The schematic value F1 = F0805B2R00FSTR is confirmed. THE REVERSE-BATTERY CORRECTNESS NOTE IS CORRECT AND IS THE BEST PART OF THIS FINDING: both D1 pins sit on Net-(BT1-+) and GND, upstream of F1 (F1 pad1 is also Net-(BT1-+)), and the pin-1-is-cathode convention is confirmed by D2, whose pad1 = /VFILT and pad2 = VBATT (it must conduct VBATT -> VFILT to be useful). So on reverse insertion the loop is battery -> D1 -> battery and never crosses F1; the 1SS355VM small-signal switching diode absorbs it alone. WHAT DOES NOT SURVIVE AS AN EFFICIENCY FINDING: the saving is a difference of two published MAXIMA, which is not a bound on the actual difference - the true installed delta could be anywhere from negative to ~30 mOhm. Worse, the 0.080 Ohm is specified at 10% of rated current (0.2 A) and 25 C; the element self-heats, and the same table's 220 mV max at 2 A implies <=110 mOhm at 2 A, so at the real 490 mA the resistance sits somewhere in an unpublished band between those points. Also 480 mA should be 490 mA (MouseBiteLabs measured at a 2.4 V bench supply, so 1175 mW / 2.4 V = 490 mA). Verdict: keep the D1 observation as a standalone correctness item; discard the milliwatt numbers as unverifiable. The finding's own conclusion - measure first, and change PTC1 rather than F1 - is the right call and I agree with it.

findings.title: Output and input capacitance is comfortably adequate for LTC3527 stability even fully derated — but the 43 uF on VOUT3 makes the part leave Burst Mode at a lighter load than it otherwise would
findings.current_part: VOUT3 carries C42 22 uF (0805) + C2 10 uF (0603) + C23 10 uF (0603) + C22 1 uF (0603) = 43 uF nominal. VOUT5 carries C21 22 uF (0805) + C72 0.1 uF. VIN (VCC) carries C37 10 uF (0603) only. LTC3527 datasheet, Output and Input Capacitor Selection: "A 4.7uF to 10uF output capacitor is sufficient for most applications. Larger values up to 22uF may be used", "The internal loop compensation of the LTC3527/LTC3527-1 is designed to be stable with output capacitor values of 4.7uF or greater", and "A 2.2uF input capacitor is sufficient for most applications, although larger values may be used without limitations."
findings.proposal: No change. I considered and rejected reducing the VOUT3 bulk capacitance to raise the Burst threshold: the datasheet warns that "larger output capacitor values may cause this transition to occur at lighter loads", but VOUT3's idle load (~37 mA stock, ~49 mA with the ClockxControl) is above the leave-burst threshold at 1.2 MHz regardless of capacitance, so removing capacitance would buy nothing and would cost transient response.
findings.benefit: Zero mW — this is a verification result, and the reviewer should know the capacitor bank is not a problem so it stops being a suspect. Stability arithmetic: even at a pessimistic 70% DC-bias loss on the 22 uF 0805 at 3.336 V and 50% on the 10 uF 0603s, effective capacitance on VOUT3 is 6.6 + 5 + 5 + 0.9 = ~17 uF, more than 3x the 4.7 uF stability minimum. Ripple arithmetic in the mode the board actually runs (fixed-frequency CCM at 212 mA out): dV = dI/(8 f C_eff) = 0.1154/(8 x 1.2e6 x 17e-6) = 0.7 mV, plus ESR x dI ~= 10 mOhm x 0.115 = 1.2 mV; and the output cap's own RMS ripple current is I_out x sqrt(D/(1-D)) = 0.212 x 0.601 = 127 mA rms, which in a 22 uF X5R 0805 with ~10 mOhm ESR dissipates 0.16 mW. Nothing here is marginal. C40/C41 = 15 pF across the 1.78 M top resistors are exactly the datasheet's prescription, verbatim: "add a small feedforward capacitor across the top resistor of the feedback divider [from VOUT1 (VOUT2) to FB1 (FB2)]. A typical value of 15pF will generally suffice." Correct as designed.
findings.risk: UNVERIFIED: the exact MPN of C21/C42 could not be retrieved — the AGBM-01 BOM points at a Digi-Key short link (digikey.com/short/cfmmbvdh) and Digi-Key returned 503/403 to this session, and Murata/TDK/Samsung DC-bias viewers all returned 403 or empty data. The 70%/50% derating figures above are therefore generic X5R assumptions, not manufacturer curves — but the conclusion is insensitive to them, since even a 90% loss on every capacitor leaves 4.3 uF on VOUT3 and 2.2 uF on VOUT5, and only the VOUT5 case would then be below the 4.7 uF minimum. If you want certainty, pin the MPN and check its bias curve; a 22 uF 0805 in 10 V rating instead of 6.3 V would remove the question entirely at the same footprint.
findings.verify_reason: Every datasheet quote is verbatim in the copy I fetched: 'A 4.7uF to 10uF output capacitor is sufficient for most applications. Larger values up to 22uF may be used to obtain lower output voltage ripple and improve transient response'; 'The internal loop compensation of the LTC3527/LTC3527-1 is designed to be stable with output capacitor values of 4.7uF or greater'; 'A 2.2uF input capacitor is sufficient for most applications, although larger values may be used without limitations'; 'add a small feedforward capacitor across the top resistor of the feedback divider [from VOUT1 (VOUT2) to FB1 (FB2)]. A typical value of 15pF will generally suffice'; and 'Note that larger output capacitor values may cause this transition to occur at lighter loads'. The BOM confirms C40/C41 = 15 pF across the 1.78 M top resistors, and the rail cap inventory (VOUT3 = 22u+10u+10u+1u, VOUT5 = 22u+0.1u, VCC = 10u) matches. The decision not to strip capacitance is right. THE UNCERTAINTY CLAIM IS WRONG AND SO IS THE REMEDY. The finding says the MPN of C21/C42 'could not be retrieved' because 'Digi-Key returned 503/403 to this session', and then works from a generic 6.3 V X5R with a 70% bias loss and suggests 'a 22 uF 0805 in 10 V rating instead of 6.3 V would remove the question entirely'. I resolved the very same short link from the AGBM-01 BOM (digikey.com/short/cfmmbvdh) and it lands on Murata GRM21BR61E226ME44K: 22 uF, 25 V, X5R, 0805 (independently corroborated - the sibling GRM21BR61E226ME44L is listed by Digi-Key, Mouser, Newark and RS as 22 uF 25 V X5R 0805). The board already uses a 25 V part. At 3.34 V the bias is 13% of rating, where DC-bias loss is nowhere near 70%, so effective capacitance on VOUT3 is well above the 17 uF the finding computed, its 4.7 uF stability check has far more margin than stated, and its proposed 10 V upgrade is moot - the installed part is already better than the fix. Conclusion (capacitors are not a suspect) stands and is stronger; the caveat and the recommendation are obsolete.

findings.title: The "boost with VIN approaching VOUT" hypothesis is closed: VIN never reaches VOUT3 = 3.336 V on this board, so it is not the 29 mW
findings.current_part: VOUT3 = V_FB x (1 + R23/R55) = 1.20 x (1 + 1.78M/1.00M) = 3.336 V, using the LTC3527's specified feedback voltage of 1.20 V typ (1.176-1.224 V over temperature). LTC3527 maximum duty cycle 85% min / 90% typ at V_FB = 1 V; minimum duty cycle 0% at V_FB = 1.3 V; the datasheet has an explicit "VIN > VOUT Operation" section stating the part "will maintain output voltage regulation even when the input voltage is above one or both of the desired output voltages" but that "this mode is less efficient and will dissipate more power".
findings.proposal: None. Documenting the negative result so nobody chases it again.
findings.benefit: Zero mW, but it removes the leading hypothesis. Two fresh alkaline AAs are 3.2 V open circuit, which is 136 mV BELOW VOUT3 = 3.336 V, and two eneloop pro NiMH (the cells MouseBiteLabs actually tested with, per the Required-Parts wiki) are 2.6-2.8 V fresh and ~2.5 V under load. So VIN < VOUT3 at every point of every discharge curve and the converter is always boosting; the datasheet's VIN > VOUT penalty never engages. Note also that AGBM-02 does not win here either — it is buck-boost, which would be the advantage if VIN did exceed VOUT, but on this board that advantage is never cashed. The gap has to be explained by light-load mode behaviour and switch resistance instead, which is what findings ltc3527-shared-burst-decision and ltc3527-channel-assignment-backwards do.
findings.risk: One residual caveat worth knowing for alkaline users: at VIN = 3.2 V the required boost duty cycle is D = 1 - 3.2/3.336 = 4.1%, which at 1.2 MHz is a 34 ns on-time. The datasheet specifies a minimum duty cycle of 0% and does not publish a minimum on-time, so regulation is claimed, but expect pulse-skipping and elevated output ripple in the first few minutes of a fresh alkaline pack. UNVERIFIED — no minimum on-time figure exists in the datasheet to check this against.
findings.verify_reason: I checked every element independently. Divider: BOM and schematic both give R23 = 1.78 M and R55 = 1 M in 0603; the datasheet EC table reads 'Feedback Voltage FB1, FB2 [l] 1.176 1.20 1.224 V', so VOUT3 = 1.20 x (1 + 1.78/1.00) = 3.336 V nominal. Duty limits confirmed: 'Maximum Duty Cycle VFB1,2 = 1V [l] 85 90 %' and 'Minimum Duty Cycle VFB1,2 = 1.3V [l] 0%'. The 'VIN > VOUT Operation' section exists and says exactly what is quoted - the part maintains regulation, all VINs must be common, and 'this mode is less efficient and will dissipate more power'. I also confirmed the UNVERIFIED flag is honest: the datasheet publishes a minimum duty cycle of 0% and no minimum on-time anywhere. Two additional supports the finding did not use, both of which strengthen it: (a) the board's own UVLO, U3 = TPS3840DL20 monitoring /VFILT and driving /EN -> SHDN2, has VIT- = 2.0 V per TI's orderable table, so the operating VIN window is roughly 2.0-3.2 V, entirely below 3.336 V; and (b) MouseBiteLabs' wiki states the measurements were taken at 'a benchtop supply providing 2.4V'. One caveat worth adding rather than a defect: 3.336 V is nominal and the FB reference band is 1.176-1.224 V, so a low-corner part regulates VOUT3 to 3.27 V, which against a 3.2 V fresh alkaline pack leaves only ~70 mV - so 'never' is a nominal statement, and a worst-corner part with fresh alkalines can graze the region the finding closes. That does not change the conclusion that the 29 mW gap is not explained by VIN > VOUT.

findings.title: What the ClockxControl actually costs through this converter: +62 mA on VOUT3 buys 165 mW of useful load for 247 mW at the battery — a 67% chain efficiency
findings.current_part: ECO-6 puts the ClockxControl's V+ on P1 pad S1 = VDD3, which the netlist shows is fed from VOUT3 through U18 (TPS22917 load switch). The overclock's extra core current lands on VDD2 = 2.5 V, produced by U8 (NCV8164ASN250T1G) whose input pin 1 is VOUT3. An LDO passes its output current 1:1 to its input, so BOTH the module's own 12 mA and the overclock's extra core current appear on VOUT3 and pass through L2, converter 2, PTC1 and F1.
findings.proposal: No component change in this finding — it is the quantification the review asked for, and it sizes the prize for the other findings. Combine with ptc1-lorho-1a5-swap (-17 mW), ltc3527-channel-assignment-backwards (-13 mW) and l2-3u3-raise-burst-threshold (-3 mW) to recover ~33 mW of the ~44 mW converter-path tax.
findings.benefit: Step by step at the in-use operating point (VIN 2.45 V, VOUT3 3.336 V, screen at max brightness). Extra load: 12 mA on VDD3 = 12 x 3.336 = 40.0 mW, plus a central 50 mA on VDD2 = 50 x 3.336 = 166.8 mW drawn from VOUT3, of which only 2.5 x 50 = 125 mW reaches VDD2 and 41.8 mW is burned as heat in U8. Total extra VOUT3 load = 62 mA = 206.8 mW. Converter tax: extra conduction loss in converter 2 alone = (0.084434 - 0.042823) x 0.6934 = 28.9 mW, i.e. the boost burns an extra 29 mW just to move that current. At ~89% overall converter efficiency the 207 mW of rail power costs 232 mW at VCC, so input current rises by 232/2.4 = 97 mA, from 480 to 577 mA. Input path tax: with a central 0.080 Ohm PTC + 0.070 Ohm fuse = 0.150 Ohm, loss goes 0.480^2 x 0.15 = 34.6 mW to 0.577^2 x 0.15 = 49.9 mW, +15.3 mW. TOTAL at the battery: ~247 mW extra for 165 mW of useful load (125 mW into the AGB core/SRAM and 40 mW into the module), a 67% chain efficiency; ~44 mW of that 247 mW is pure converter-path and input-path loss. Equivalently, every extra milliamp on VOUT3 costs the battery about 1.6x its face value once the boost, the LDO drop, the PTC and the fuse are counted. On the 1175 mW in-use figure that takes the console to ~1422 mW and cuts the 5h20m worst-case battery life to roughly 4h25m.
findings.risk: The biggest uncertainty is where insideGadgets' 40-60 mA actually sits. They publish it as a console-level increase, not a per-rail one. FLAGGED as instructed: if some of it is on VDD3 or VDD35 rather than VDD2, the LDO's 41.8 mW of waste shrinks but the VOUT3 total does not change, because every one of those rails is fed from VOUT3 — so the converter and input-path numbers above are robust to that ambiguity and only the LDO term moves. At the low end (+40 mA) the totals scale to ~205 mW / ~37 mW of loss; at the high end (+60 mA) to ~271 mW / ~48 mW. The 89% converter efficiency is read off datasheet Fig. G05 and the 0.150 Ohm input resistance is a central value between published bounds, both stated above.
findings.verify_reason: THE STRUCTURAL CLAIM IS CORRECT AND I CONFIRMED IT INDEPENDENTLY. The powernet dump shows VDD3 is fed by U18 (TPS22917) pins 5/6 from VOUT3, and P1 pad S1 is on VDD3 - so the module's V+ does hang off VOUT3. U8 (NCV8164ASN250T1G) pin 1 is VOUT3 and pin 5 is VDD2, and VDD2 carries U1 pins 44/65/115/117 and U2 pins 12/16/37 - so the AGB core and SRAM are LDO'd down from VOUT3 and an LDO does pass load current 1:1. Everything therefore does route through L2, converter 2, PTC1 and F1. NCV8164 headroom is fine (onsemi datasheet: 2.5 V option dropout 125 mV typ / 200 mV max at 300 mA, Iq 30 uA typ). THE CENTRAL NUMBER IS PROBABLY DOUBLE-COUNTED. insideGadgets' exact sentence is 'Consumes about 12mA of additional current and when the GBA/GBC/DMG is overclocked, it too will use 40-60mA more.' The subject of the second clause is the console, and no measurement node is given. The finding takes the 40-60 mA as a VOUT3-rail current and then inflates it by 1.6x through the LDO drop, the boost and the input path. If the figure is battery-side - the more natural reading of a vendor quoting how much more current a console draws - the correct arithmetic is +50 mA at 2.4 V = 120 mW at the battery, input rising 490 -> 540 mA, and 'about 247 mW extra for 165 mW of useful load' becomes ~160 mW extra with almost none of it new conversion loss. The finding's explicit assertion that 'the converter and input-path numbers above are robust to that ambiguity' is FALSE: they move by roughly 35%, and every downstream figure in the review (577 mA input current, 212 mA on VOUT3, the 4h25m battery life, the 44 mW converter-path tax) inherits it. Secondary corrections: VIN should be 2.4 V not 2.45 V per the wiki, so the base input current is 490 mA not 480 mA; and the 89% efficiency read off G05 is closer to 90-92% on my own read of the same graph. What survives unchanged: the topology argument that every milliamp added anywhere on VDD2, VDD3 or VAUD lands on VOUT3 and is paid for at the battery with a multiplier - that part is solid and is the useful content. The multiplier itself needs a measurement, not a datasheet.

findings.title: VOUT3 regulates to 3.336 V; trimming R55 to 1.02 M gives 3.294 V and hands back a few mW of NCV8164 dropout at overclocked core currents
findings.current_part: R23 = 1.78 M, R55 = 1.00 M, both 0603. VOUT3 = 1.20 x (1 + 1.78/1.00) = 3.336 V. This is exactly the divider from the LTC3527 datasheet's own front-page 3.3 V application, so it is not a mistake — it is simply 36 mV above the 3.3 V the AGB actually wants. Divider current = 3.336/2.78M = 1.20 uA, so the divider itself costs 4 uW and there is nothing to gain there.
findings.proposal: R55 1.00 M -> 1.02 M (standard E96, same 0603 land, same tolerance class): VOUT3 = 1.20 x (1 + 1.78/1.02) = 3.294 V. R23 unchanged, C41 unchanged.
findings.benefit: Small and honest. The 42 mV reduction is dropped straight out of U8's (VOUT3 - 2.5 V) dissipation. At an estimated 75 mA on VDD2 with the overclock at 1.75x (25 mA base plus 50 mA), the LDO stops wasting 0.075 x 0.042 = 3.15 mW, which at ~89% converter efficiency is ~3.5 mW at VCC. Without the overclock, at an estimated 25 mA on VDD2, it is 1.05 mW at the rail, ~1.2 mW at VCC. The VDD3 loads also see 42 mV less, which is a further small win that I have not tried to quantify. Total: about 1 mW stock, about 3.5 mW overclocked. This is a rounding-error lever compared with the PTC and the channel swap, and I am reporting it as such.
findings.risk: My VDD2 current is an ESTIMATE (25 mA base) and it is the weak link in the arithmetic — if VDD2 idles at 10 mA the stock saving halves. Functionally the risk is low: the original GBA runs VDD3 at 3.3 V, so 3.294 V is if anything more correct than 3.336 V, it is inside any 3.3 V +/-5% specification, and it costs the NCV8164 only 42 mV of the ~800 mV headroom it has over its 2.5 V output. The one thing to check is your cartridge: VDD3 feeds P1 pad S1 and some flash carts are fussy, though 3.294 V is well inside spec. If the ClockxControl module itself has a minimum supply requirement near 3.3 V, verify it before making this change.
findings.verify_reason: The mechanics check out. R23 = 1.78 M and R55 = 1 M confirmed in both the schematic and the BOM, both on R_0603_1608Metric_Boxed; VFB = 1.20 V typ confirmed; VOUT3 = 3.336 V; 1.02 M is a standard E96 value and gives 1.20 x (1 + 1.78/1.02) = 3.294 V, a 42 mV reduction. The divider-current note is right: 3.336/2.78 M = 1.20 uA = 4.0 uW, nothing to recover there. Drop-in on the existing 0603 land, no PCB change - confirmed. The functional risk is genuinely low: onsemi's NCV8164 datasheet gives the 2.5 V option 125 mV typ / 200 mV max dropout at 300 mA, so trimming 42 mV out of 836 mV of headroom is a non-event. I also considered and REJECTED an objection I initially had - that the +/-2% FB tolerance (1.176-1.224 V) swamps a 42 mV trim. It does not: changing the divider ratio shifts VOUT3 by -1.26% on every individual board regardless of where its reference sits, so the saving is deterministic per unit. WHAT IS WRONG IS THE MAGNITUDE. The entire benefit is linear in the VDD2 current, and both figures used (25 mA base, 75 mA overclocked) are stated estimates with no basis given - no measurement, no datasheet, no derivation from the 170 mW / 1175 mW envelope. The finding admits this is 'the weak link'. It is not a weak link, it is the whole calculation. An honest range given what is actually known is roughly 0.5-3.5 mW, and it should be reported as 'about a milliwatt, unmeasured' rather than 1.2/3.5. The unquantified 'VDD3 loads also see 42 mV less' is real but tiny - CMOS dynamic power scales as V^2, so ~2.5% of that branch. Verdict: correct, drop-in, and honestly labelled as a rounding-error lever; the specific numbers are not supported.

findings.title: F1 and PTC1 carry the PCB Value "0467001.NR" in the layout while the schematic and published BOM say F0805B2R00FSTR and 0805L075SLYR
findings.current_part: Parsing the footprint Value properties out of the layouts: in BOTH the stock agbm01/AGBM-01_AA_1-2.kicad_pcb and the fork's x/agbm-01-ram-desalvage/AGBM-01_AA_1-2_GBE-plus.kicad_pcb, F1 and PTC1 both have Value = "0467001.NR". The schematic AGBM-01_AA_1-2.kicad_sch and MouseBiteLabs' published AGBM-01 BOM give F1 = F0805B2R00FSTR (2 A fuse) and PTC1 = 0805L075SLYR (0.75 A PPTC). 0467001.NR is a Littelfuse Nano2 1 A cartridge fuse, which is neither part and does not fit a 0805 land.
findings.proposal: Update the Value property on both footprints to match the schematic. Purely a documentation fix, no electrical change.
findings.benefit: Zero mW. It matters because anyone generating a BOM or a pick-and-place from the layout rather than the schematic — which is the normal JLCPCB/PCBWay assembly flow — would order or place the wrong parts on the two components that carry the entire board current. It also means the layout's Value fields cannot be trusted as a cross-check anywhere else, which is worth knowing when reviewing the rest of the board.
findings.risk: None. Note this defect exists upstream in MouseBiteLabs' own AGBM-01 files, not just in the fork, so fixing it locally will show up as a diff against upstream. Worth reporting upstream.
findings.verify_reason: THE DEFECT IS REAL - I reproduced it myself rather than trusting the report. Parsing footprint blocks out of both layouts: agbm01/AGBM-01_AA_1-2.kicad_pcb gives F1 Value='0467001.NR' FP='Bucketmouse:Fuse_0805_2012Metric' and PTC1 Value='0467001.NR' same footprint; x/agbm-01-ram-desalvage/AGBM-01_AA_1-2_GBE-plus.kicad_pcb gives identical results. Meanwhile agbm01/AGBM-01_AA_1-2.kicad_sch carries (property "Value" "F0805B2R00FSTR") and (property "Value" "0805L075SLYR"), and MouseBiteLabs' published AGBM-01 README BOM lists F1 = F0805B2R00FSTR and PTC1 = 0805L075SLYR. So the layout Value fields do contradict the schematic and the published BOM on the two components carrying the entire board current, and the defect is upstream, not introduced by the fork. THE IDENTIFICATION OF 0467001.NR IS WRONG, AND THE ERROR MATTERS. It is not 'a Littelfuse Nano2 1 A cartridge fuse' and it does not fail to fit an 0805 land. Newark's page for 0467001.NR (part 12J3738) gives 'Package/Case Size: 0603 [1608 Metric], Current Rating 1 A, Voltage Rating 32 V, Series: 467' - a surface-mount very-fast-acting chip fuse. Because it is 0603 it WOULD sit on the 0805 land and solder, which makes the assembly hazard worse than the finding argues, not better: a house that BOMs and places from the layout would fit a 1 A / 32 V fast-acting fuse in both the 2 A fuse position and the 0.75 A PPTC position, the board would build and boot, and the fault would only show up as nuisance blowing under load - a latent failure rather than an obvious one. Supporting evidence that upstream property fields are generally untrustworthy: AGBM-02's schematic assigns U5/U13 the footprint 'Package_SON:VSON-10-1EP_3x3mm_P0.5mm_EP1.2x2mm' while its PCB actually uses 'Bucketmouse:VREG_TPS63802DLAR' - a second stale property field in the same family of designs. Fix and report upstream as recommended; just describe the wrong part correctly.

findings.title: Replace U8 with a buck-boost fed straight from VCC — skips the boost entirely for the core rail, the single largest lever in this domain
findings.current_part: U8 = NCV8164ASN250T1G, SOT-23-5 (onsemi TSOP-5, CASE 483), fixed 2.5 V, VIN 1.6-5.5 V, Iq 30 uA typ / 40 uA max at IOUT = 0, dropout 125 mV typ / 200 mV max at 300 mA for the 2.5 V option, current limit 350 mA min. Fed from VOUT3 = 3.336 V, so its efficiency is fixed at (2.5/3.336) x (30/30.03) = 74.87%. Cascaded with the LTC3527 boost (eta 0.92 from datasheet curve G05, Burst, VOUT2 = 3.3 V, 1.2 MHz, VIN 2.4 V, 10-100 mA), the battery-to-core chain efficiency is 0.92 x 0.7487 = 0.689.
findings.proposal: TPS63900DSK — synchronous buck-boost, VIN 1.8-5.5 V, VOUT 1.8-5 V programmable in 100 mV steps by two config resistors, >400 mA output for VI >= 2.0 V, 75 nA quiescent current, 60 nA shutdown, 10-pin WSON 2.5 mm x 2.5 mm, external 2.2 uH inductor + single 22 uF output capacitor, 21 mm2 total solution size. Datasheet Figure 8-2 shows the VO = 2.5 V trace reaching ~0.47 A capability at VI = 1.8 V and ~0.85 A at 2.3 V — about 10x what VDD2 needs. Its headline feature matters here: 'Single-mode operation — eliminates mode transitions between buck, buck-boost and boost operation / Low output ripple', which is exactly the property you want on a rail that sits near VIN ~= VOUT for most of an alkaline discharge. Alternative: TPS63802 (VIN 1.3-5.5 V, VOUT 1.8-5.2 V adjustable, 2 A, 11 uA Iq, 10-pin VSON-HR 3.0 x 2.0 mm, 0.47 uH inductor, 22 uF minimum output cap, 21.5 mm2) — the part MouseBiteLabs already uses on AGBM-02, so it is proven in this exact console, but with 11 uA vs 75 nA of Iq and explicit buck/buck-boost/boost mode transitions.
findings.benefit: Battery-to-core chain today: 0.92 (boost) x 0.7487 (LDO) = 0.689. Direct buck-boost at eta = 0.89. At 1x, core = 2.5 V x 30 mA = 75 mW: 75/0.689 = 108.9 mW at the battery today vs 75/0.89 = 84.3 mW, saving 24.6 mW. At 1.75x, core = 2.5 V x 48 mA = 120 mW: 120/0.689 = 174.2 mW vs 120/0.89 = 134.8 mW, saving 39.4 mW. Range across my 44-53 mA overclock band: 36.1 to 43.5 mW. The 0.89 figure is read off the TPS63900 curves by bracketing: VO = 2.5 V is not plotted, but Figure 8-6 (VO = 1.8 V) at VI = 2.5 V runs 89-90% over 10-100 mA and Figure 8-7 (VO = 3.3 V) at VI = 2.5 V runs 90-91% over the same range, so 89% for VO = 2.5 V across the 2.1-3.2 V pack range is a fair and slightly conservative reading. 24.6 mW is 14% of the 170 mW idle figure; 39.4 mW is 3.4% of the 1175 mW in-use peak.
findings.risk: Four costs, in descending order of how likely they are to kill it. (1) SEQUENCING — U8's PGOOD pin (pad 4) drives /PG_2V5, which is the enable input of both U4 (pad 3) and U18 (pad 3), implementing MBL's annotated 'CPU Power sequence: VDD2 >> VDD3 >> VDD5'. The TPS63900 pin list is EN, SEL, CFG1, CFG2, CFG3, VOUT, LX2, GND, LX1, VIN — there is no power-good output, and neither has the TPS63802. You must regenerate /PG_2V5, e.g. a fourth TPS3840 watching VDD2. That is a schematic change with its own part, not a footprint swap. (2) NOISE ON THE CORE RAIL — MouseBiteLabs' own root-schematic annotation, placed above U8, reads 'Audio seems to sound best when noise on VDD2 is minimized'. That is the designer telling you, from experience with this exact console, that VDD2 ripple is audible through the CPU's audio path. A burst-mode converter's switching frequency falls with load; at 30-50 mA the TPS63900 burst frequency is a few hundred kHz (Figure 8-3), safely above audio, but this must be verified by ear, not by multimeter. (3) AREA — 21 mm2 of inductor, 22 uF cap and IC, on a board whose centre 18.65 x 12.00 mm is now spoken for by the ClockxControl, plus a new VCC route across to it. (4) You lose the LDO's 260 Ohm active output discharge on VDD2, which currently gives a clean power-down of a salvaged CPU.
findings.verify_reason: I fetched and parsed every datasheet myself rather than trusting the citations. NCV8164 (onsemi rev.5, Mar 2025): TSOP-5 pin table 1=IN, 2=GND, 3=EN, 4=PG, 5=OUT confirmed; Iq 30 typ/40 max uA at IOUT=0; dropout for VOUT(NOM)=2.5 V is 125 mV typ/200 mV max at IOUT=300 mA; current limit 350 mA min; VIN 1.6-5.5 V; TSOP-5 = CASE 483. So 2.5/3.336 = 74.94%, x(30/30.03) = 74.87% reproduces — but note the 30 uA is Iq at IOUT=0; onsemi specifies no ground-current-vs-load curve, so that term is an assumption, not a verified number. LTC3527: the finding cites curve G05 for the boost efficiency; I rendered p.4 of the datasheet and G05 is indeed 'Efficiency vs Load Current and VIN for VOUT2 = 3.3 V at 1.2 MHz', which is the right graph for this board (VOUT3 is on channel 2; U5 FSEL=GND -> 1.2 MHz; MODE=GND -> Burst). The VIN=2.4 V Burst trace reads ~92-93% over 10-100 mA, so 0.92 is fair and slightly conservative. TPS63900 (SLVSET3D): every headline spec checks out — VIN 1.8-5.5 V, VOUT 1.8-5 V in 100 mV steps, 75 nA Iq, 60 nA shutdown, 10-pin WSON DSK 2.5 x 2.5 mm, 'Tiny solution size of 21-mm2 / Small 2.2-uH inductor, single 22-uF output capacitor', and the 'Single-mode operation / Eliminates mode transitions between buck, buck-boost and boost operation / Low output ripple' bullet is verbatim. Pin list EN, SEL, CFG1, CFG2, CFG3, VOUT, LX2, GND, LX1, VIN — confirmed, no PG. I rendered p.23: Figure 8-2 VO=2.5 V trace reads ~0.46-0.47 A at VI=1.8 V and ~0.85 A at VI=2.3 V (as claimed); Figure 8-6 (VO=1.8 V) VI=2.5 V runs 89-90% over 10-100 mA (as claimed); Figure 8-7 (VO=3.3 V) VI=2.5 V actually runs ~91-94%, better than the stated 90-91%, so the 89% working figure is conservative, not optimistic. TPS63802 (SLVSEU9D): VIN 1.3-5.5 V (startup needs VI > 1.8 V), VOUT 1.8-5.2 V adjustable, 2 A for VI>=2.3 V at VO=3.3 V, 11 uA Iq, 10-pin VSON-HR 3.0 x 2.0 mm, 0.47 uH, 22 uF min output cap, 21.5 mm2, 'Defined transition points between buck, buck-boost, and boost operation modes' — all as stated. Arithmetic redone and it reproduces exactly: 0.92 x 0.7487 = 0.6888; 75/0.689 = 108.9 vs 75/0.89 = 84.3, diff 24.6; 120/0.689 = 174.2 vs 134.8, diff 39.4; 44 mA -> 36.1, 53 mA -> 43.4; 24.6/170 = 14.5%; 39.4/1175 = 3.4%. Board facts verified from the KiCad files: U8 pad 4 -> /PG_2V5, U4 pad 3 -> /PG_2V5, U18 pad 3 -> /PG_2V5, R8 100k VDD2->/PG_2V5, U8 pad 3 -> /PG_3V3 <- U5 pad 13 (PGOOD2) with R13 100k to VOUT3. Both schematic annotations exist verbatim in AGBM-01_AA_1-2.kicad_sch ('Audio seems to sound best when noise on VDD2 is minimized' at 99.06,87.63 — directly above U8 at 99.06,100.33; 'CPU Power sequence:\nVDD2 >> VDD3 >> VDD5' at 88.646,127.762). Envelope check on the load assumption: the 30 mA / 48 mA core currents carry the whole mW claim linearly and NO basis is given for either. They are at least consistent with the measured envelope — 75 mW core -> 108.9 mW at the battery is 64% of the 170 mW idle, leaving ~61 mW for VDD3, VAUD, VOUT5, the supervisors and the R9 divider, which is tight but feasible — so I cannot refute them, but they must be labelled estimates, and every mW quoted scales with them.
findings.correction: Direction and arithmetic survive; the recommended part does not. Use the TPS63802, not the TPS63900. Risk item (1) — the claim that 'there is no power-good output, and neither has the TPS63802' — is false. TPS63802 datasheet Table 7-1: pin 5 = PG, 'Power good indicator, open-drain output'; section 9.3.10: goes high-Z above 95% of nominal, driven low below 90% typical — the SAME thresholds as the NCV8164's PG (95%/90%) — sinks 1 mA, requires a pull-up 'to any voltage rail less than 5.5 V', and TI writes verbatim 'The PG signal can be used to sequence multiple rails by connecting it to the EN pin of other converters.' R8's existing 100 k pull-up to VDD2 sources 25 uA, well inside 1 mA, so /PG_2V5 is regenerated with zero added parts. MouseBiteLabs already does exactly this: in AGBM-02_AA_1-1.kicad_pcb U13 (TPS63802, VOUT3) pad 5 = /PG_3V3 and U5 (TPS63802, VOUT5) pad 5 = /~RESET, and MBL's library already carries the land pattern Bucketmouse:VREG_TPS63802DLAR. Three further corrections: (a) the TPS63900 needs THREE config resistors, not two — CFG1, CFG2 and CFG3 all 'must not be left open', and SEL must also be tied; (b) '>400 mA output for VI >= 2.0 V' is specified at VO = 3.6 V (Rec. Op. Cond.) / 3.3 V (features), not at 2.5 V; (c) the area/route framing is loose — U8 sits on B.Cu at (18.4, -30.3), about 11 mm from the VCC node (C37/L2/U5, all B.Cu) and nowhere near the ClockxControl window at x 82.6-101.3, so the new VCC run is ~11 mm, not 'across the board'. One thing the finding never addresses: output capacitance. TPS63900 wants 22 uF (10 uF effective per Rec. Op. Cond.); TPS63802 wants 7 uF effective for VO > 2.3 V. VDD2 today carries C60 (10u 0603) + 4 x 1u + 5 x 0.1u, which after DC-bias derating at 2.5 V is marginal — C60 probably has to grow, an extra PCB change beyond the IC. Revised benefit with TPS63802 at ~90%: 75/0.689 - 75/0.90 = 108.9 - 83.3 = 25.6 mW at 1x; at 48 mA, 174.2 - 133.3 = 40.9 mW. Its 11 uA Iq costs 11 uA x ~2.4 V = 0.026 mW, irrelevant against a 25-41 mW prize.

findings.title: Replace U8 with a buck from VOUT3 — only 0.84 V of headroom, but D = 0.75 is a completely ordinary duty cycle and it is viable
findings.current_part: U8 = NCV8164ASN250T1G, TSOP-5/SOT-23-5, 2.5 V fixed, 74.87% efficient from VOUT3 = 3.336 V. Loss = (3.336 - 2.5) x IOUT + 3.336 x 30 uA. Thermal: theta-JA 158 C/W for TSOP-5, onsemi advise limiting TJ to 125 C, so PD(max) = (125-40)/158 = 538 mW at 40 C ambient — the part is nowhere near its limit, this is purely an efficiency problem.
findings.proposal: TPS62840DLC — 1.8 V to 6.5 V input, 750 mA, 60 nA operating quiescent current, 25 nA shutdown, output 1.8-3.3 V in 100 mV steps set by a single resistor on VSET, SON-8 package 1.5 mm x 2.0 mm, needs an external 2.2 uH inductor, 4.7 uF input cap and 10 uF output cap. It also carries a STOP pin that halts switching for a quiet supply rail, which is a genuinely useful hook on an audio-sensitive console. ALTERNATIVE with almost no area cost: TPS82740A — a MicroSiP module with the inductor and both capacitors integrated, 2.30 mm x 2.90 mm body, VIN 2.2-5.5 V, 200 mA, 360 nA Iq, output pin-selectable 1.8 V to 2.5 V in 100 mV steps (2.5 V is the top setting, exactly what VDD2 needs), lifecycle status ACTIVE on ti.com. Its 2.30 x 2.90 mm body is essentially the same area as the SOT-23-5 land pattern it would replace, and U8's nearest same-side neighbours (C2 at 3.70 mm, C60 at 3.50 mm) leave room — so this swap costs no net board area and adds no discrete inductor.
findings.benefit: Duty cycle first, since the brief asks whether 0.84 V of headroom is even viable: D = VOUT/VIN = 2.5/3.336 = 0.749. That is a mainstream buck duty cycle with a large margin to any dropout or minimum-off-time limit; the 100%-mode and dropout questions only bite when VIN - VOUT is a couple of hundred millivolts. It is viable. TPS62840 efficiency at this operating point, from datasheet Figure 18 (VOUT = 2.5 V, RSET = 11.5 kOhm to GND, PFM/PWM): at 30 mA the VIN = 3.0 V trace reads ~94% and the VIN = 3.6 V trace ~93.5%; at 50 mA both read ~94%. Our VIN is 3.336 V, between the two. I use 93% conservatively. At 1x (30 mA): LDO input = 3.336 x 30.03 = 100.2 mW; buck input = 75/0.93 = 80.6 mW; saving 19.4 mW at VOUT3 = 21.1 mW at the battery (dividing by the 0.92 boost efficiency). That is 12.4% of the 170 mW idle figure. At 1.75x (48 mA): 160.1 mW vs 129.0 mW = 31.1 mW at VOUT3 = 33.8 mW at the battery; across the 44-53 mA band, 31.0 to 36.4 mW. With the TPS82740A instead, efficiency at VOUT = 2.5 V is not plotted, but Figure 5 (VOUT = 2.1 V, VIN = 3.3 V) reads ~87.5% and Figure 6 (VOUT = 2.6 V, VIN = 3.3 V) reads ~91.5% over 10-100 mA, so ~90% for 2.5 V — giving 16.7 mW at VOUT3 / 18.2 mW at battery at 1x, and 26.8 / 29.1 mW at 1.75x.
findings.risk: Same PGOOD blocker as the buck-boost option and it is the decisive one: neither the TPS62840 (pins VIN, SW, GND, VSET, VOS, EN, STOP, MODE) nor the TPS82740 (EN, VSEL1-3, CTRL, VIN, VOUT, LOAD, GND) has a power-good output, and U8's PG is what enables U4 and U18. You must add a supervisor to regenerate /PG_2V5. Second, this is double conversion — battery to boost (0.92) to buck (0.93) = 0.856 overall, versus 0.89 for a single buck-boost straight off VCC, so it wins less than option 1 for similar effort; its only advantage is that it does not need a new VCC route and, in the TPS82740A form, no new inductor. Third, switching ripple lands on the CPU core rail, against MBL's explicit note that VDD2 noise is audible. Fourth, TPS82740A is capped at 200 mA — fine for 48 mA, but it removes headroom if the core current estimate is badly wrong. Neither part is a drop-in on the SOT-23-5 land pattern: both need a new footprint, so this is a PCB revision.
findings.verify_reason: Redone independently. Duty cycle: 2.5/3.336 = 0.7494 — an ordinary buck duty, and the finding is right that dropout and minimum-off-time only bite when VIN-VOUT is a couple hundred mV. TPS62840 (SLVSEC6D): I parsed the datasheet directly because a summarizer returned hallucinated numbers for it. Verified: 60 nA operating Iq, 25 nA shutdown, VIN 1.8-6.5 V, up to 750 mA, 16 selectable output voltages via a single VSET resistor, DLC (SON-8) body 1.5 mm x 2 mm, typical application uses L = 2.2 uH, CI = 4.7 uF, CO = 10 uF, STOP pin present. The VSET table confirms RSET = 11.5 k -> 2.5 V. I rendered p.19 and Figure 18 is exactly 'Efficiency Power Save Mode VOUT = 2.5 V', condition line 'RSET = 11.5 kOhm to GND', in-plot label 'VOUT=2.5V PFM/PWM Operation' — the citation is correct. Reading the curves at 30 mA: VIN = 3.0 V is ~93.5-94%, VIN = 3.6 V is ~93%; at 50 mA both ~94%. The finding's readings are accurate to within half a point and its working value of 93% is conservative. TPS82740A (SLVSCE3A): 360 nA typical Iq, up to 200 mA, VIN 2.2-5.5 V, 'Pin-Selectable Output Voltages in 100-mV Steps', body 2.30 mm x 2.90 mm MicroSiP, total solution < 6.7 mm2. The output range is explicitly 'from 1.8 V to 2.5 V (TPS82740A) and 2.6 V to 3.3 V (TPS82740B)' — so 2.5 V really is the top A-suffix setting, as claimed. ti.com/product/TPS82740A shows lifecycle status ACTIVE, so the sourcing claim holds. Nine bumps: VOUT, LOAD, VSEL3, VIN, EN, VSEL1, VSEL2, CTRL, GND — no PG, as the finding says. NCV8164 thermal claims verified: theta-JA 158 C/W for TSOP-5, and onsemi's Applications Information says verbatim 'For reliable operation junction temperature should be limited to +125 C', giving PD(max) = (125-40)/158 = 538 mW at TA = 40 C. Arithmetic reproduced: 3.336 x 30.03 mA = 100.2 mW; 75/0.93 = 80.6 mW; 19.5 mW at VOUT3, /0.92 = 21.2 mW at the battery (finding says 21.1); 21.2/170 = 12.4% as stated. At 48 mA: 160.2 vs 129.0 = 31.2 -> 33.9 mW. TPS82740A at 90%: 16.9 -> 18.4 mW and 26.9 -> 29.2 mW, matching. Double-conversion figure 0.92 x 0.93 = 0.856 vs 0.89 confirmed. Footprint honesty confirmed against the BOM: U8's footprint is Bucketmouse:SOT-23-5 and neither candidate lands on it — the finding says so explicitly and grades this a PCB revision, which is correct.
findings.correction: Numbers essentially stand; the framing of the blocker does not, and one band endpoint is wrong. (1) The PGOOD blocker is genuine for these two specific parts — I confirmed neither TPS62840 (VIN, GND, VSET, VOS, SW, MODE, EN, STOP on the DLC SON-8) nor TPS82740 (VOUT, LOAD, VSEL3, VIN, EN, VSEL1, VSEL2, CTRL, GND) has a power-good output — but the finding presents it as blocking the switcher approach generally, and it does not: the TPS63802 has an open-drain PG on pin 5 with 95%/90% thresholds, and MBL already uses it for exactly this sequencing role on AGBM-02. So this is an argument against these two candidates, not against replacing U8. (2) Top of the overclock band: at 53 mA I get 3.336 x 53.03 = 176.9 mW in the LDO vs 132.5/0.93 = 142.5 mW in the buck, a 34.4 mW saving at VOUT3 = 37.4 mW at the battery, not the 36.4 mW stated. The 44 mA end (31.1 mW) reproduces. (3) TPS82740A bracketing is looser than presented: Figure 5 is TPS82740A at VOUT = 2.1 V (~87.5% at VIN = 3.3 V) but Figure 6 is TPS82740**B** at VOUT = 2.6 V (~91.5%) — a different device. Interpolating 90% for 2.5 V across a device boundary carries roughly +/-2 points, so the 18.2 / 29.1 mW figures should be quoted with that spread. (4) Not addressed: the TPS62840 requires a 10 uF output capacitor; VDD2 today has C60 (10 uF, 0603) plus 4 x 1u and 5 x 0.1u, and a 10 uF 0603 at 2.5 V DC bias derates well below its marking — C60 likely has to grow, an extra change on top of the new IC footprint.

findings.title: Lower VOUT3 from 3.336 V to ~3.23 V by changing one resistor — the cheapest change on the board, and honestly worth only 4-10 mW
findings.current_part: R23 = 1.78 M and R55 = 1.00 M, both R_0603_1608Metric_Boxed, forming the LTC3527 FB2 divider. LTC3527 datasheet: 'Feedback Voltage FB1, FB2 | 1.176 | 1.20 | 1.224 V' and 'The output voltage can be adjusted from 1.6V to 5.25V by VOUT1 = 1.2[1 + R1/R2]'. So VOUT3 = 1.20 x (1 + 1.78/1.00) = 3.336 V. The two LDOs regulate to a fixed 2.5 V, so every millivolt VOUT3 comes down is a millivolt less dropped across U8 and U4.
findings.proposal: Change R23 from 1.78 M to 1.69 M (E96, same 0603 land pattern): VOUT3 = 1.20 x 2.69 = 3.228 V. More aggressive option R23 = 1.65 M gives 1.20 x 2.65 = 3.180 V. Nothing else on the board changes — this is a one-resistor value change on the existing footprint, the only genuinely drop-in item in this domain.
findings.benefit: Saving = delta-V x (I_U8 + I_U4), because both LDO outputs are pinned at 2.5 V. With R23 = 1.69 M, delta-V = 0.108 V. At 1x idle (30 mA on U8 + ~5 mA on U4 = 35 mA): 0.108 x 35 = 3.8 mW at VOUT3 = 4.1 mW at the battery, 2.4% of the 170 mW idle. At 1.75x with audio at max volume (48 + 40 mA = 88 mA): 0.108 x 88 = 9.5 mW = 10.3 mW at the battery. With R23 = 1.65 M (delta-V = 0.156 V) it becomes 5.9 mW and 14.9 mW respectively. Now the floor analysis the brief asked for — every load on VOUT3 and VDD3, with its verified minimum supply. (a) U8 and U4 need 2.5 V plus dropout plus PSRR headroom. Dropout for the 2.5 V TSOP-5 option is 125 mV typ / 200 mV max AT 300 mA; the pass element is resistive in dropout, so R_pass = 0.417 Ohm typ / 0.667 Ohm max, giving ~20 mV typ / 32 mV max at 48 mA. Dropout is NOT the binding constraint. PSRR is: onsemi specify the whole electrical table, PSRR included, at VIN = VOUT(NOM) + 0.5 V, so keeping >= 0.5 V of headroom preserves the datasheet 83/85/80/61 dB at 100 Hz/1 kHz/10 kHz/100 kHz. That sets an LDO floor of VOUT3 >= 3.0 V WORST CASE, not nominal. (b) U16 SN74HC02PWR: recommended VCC 2 V to 6 V — no constraint. (c) U15 SN74LVC1G332: recommended VCC 1.65 V to 5.5 V — no constraint. (d) U18 and U12 TPS22917: VIN 1 V to 5.5 V, rON ~100 mOhm at 3.3 V, so 6 mV of drop at 60 mA and VDD3 = VOUT3 for all practical purposes — no constraint. (e) The binding constraint is the salvaged AGB CPU's VDD3 pins (U1.1, U1.103, U1.124), the AGB SRAM, and the cartridge — MBL's own annotation puts an Everdrive at '3.3V@~50mA' on this rail. Worst case with R23 = 1.69 M: 3.228 x 0.98 (FB tolerance) x 0.98 (two 1% resistors) = 3.10 V minimum, i.e. VDD3 no worse than -6% on a nominal 3.3 V rail, and 0.60 V of LDO headroom still retained. That is the whole case for the change and the whole case against going further.
findings.risk: You are buying 4-10 mW by shaving margin on a salvaged CPU's I/O rail and on whatever cartridge is inserted. Nothing in a datasheet forbids 3.23 V; the AGB CPU and SRAM are irreplaceable parts with no published minimum VDD3, so this is judgement, not specification. Two second-order effects I am deliberately NOT counting as savings: lowering VDD3 also lowers the CPU I/O and cart switching power (goes as V^2), but that comes with slower edges and less noise margin, so it is a functional change, not free efficiency. Also unverified: the ClockxControl's V+ supply range. insideGadgets publish the current draw and the module dimensions but no supply voltage specification anywhere on the product page, and its V+ lands on VDD3 here. Recommendation: treat this as a build option to be validated by measuring VDD3 and running a real cart, not a default. If the console is stable it is the best mW-per-dollar change on the board; if it is not, you have risked a salvage for 4 mW.
findings.verify_reason: Every load-bearing number verified against primary sources. Board data from the BOM and netlist: R23 = 1.78 M and R55 = 1 M, both R_0603_1608Metric_Boxed, R23 pad 1 on VOUT3 and pad 2 on Net-(U5-FB2), R55 between that node and GND — the divider is as described, and a value change is a true drop-in on the existing land pattern. LTC3527 datasheet: 'Feedback Voltage FB1, FB2 | 1.176 | 1.20 | 1.224 V' and the FB1 pin description gives VOUT1 = 1.20[1 + R1/R2], so VOUT3 = 1.20 x 2.78 = 3.336 V, 1.69 M gives 3.228 V and 1.65 M gives 3.180 V — all three reproduce. E96 availability: Yageo's RC0603 series datasheet states the range covers 'E24 and E96 decade values from 1 ohm to 100 Mohm', and 1.65/1.69 are both E96 decade values, so both are stock 0603 1% parts. NCV8164: the electrical characteristics table header is 'VIN = VOUT(NOM) + 0.5 V ... unless otherwise noted', so the finding's reading that the datasheet PSRR/noise numbers are only warranted with >= 0.5 V of headroom is correct and its 3.0 V worst-case LDO floor follows. Dropout: 125 mV typ / 200 mV max at IOUT = 300 mA for the 2.5 V option -> 0.417/0.667 ohm pass element -> 20 mV typ / 32 mV max at 48 mA, confirming dropout is not the binding constraint. Downstream floors all verified: SN74HC02 recommended VCC 2 V min / 6 V max; SN74LVC1G332 recommended VCC 1.65-5.5 V operating; TPS22917 input operating range 1 V to 5.5 V with RON 90 mOhm typ / 110 mOhm max at VIN = 3.6 V, 25 C (140 mOhm max over -40 to +85 C) — so the drop at 60 mA is 5.4-8.4 mV, and the finding's '~100 mOhm, 6 mV, no constraint' conclusion holds. Arithmetic redone: 0.108 V x 35 mA = 3.78 mW at VOUT3, /0.92 = 4.11 mW at the battery (2.4% of 170 mW); 0.108 x 88 mA = 9.50 -> 10.33 mW; with 1.65 M, 0.156 x 35 = 5.46 -> 5.93 mW and 0.156 x 88 = 13.73 -> 14.92 mW. All reproduce. The finding is also honest about the two things that matter most: it declines to bank the V-squared saving on CPU I/O and cart switching, and it flags that the ClockxControl's supply range is unpublished while its V+ lands on this rail (P1 pad S1 is on VDD3, confirmed in the netlist). It is the only genuinely drop-in item in the domain and it correctly reports the prize as 4-10 mW rather than inflating it.
findings.correction: Two refinements, both in the safe direction. The worst-case tolerance stack is slightly over-pessimistic: two 1% resistors move the (1 + R1/R2) multiplier by -1.25%, not -2% (1 + (1.69 x 0.99)/(1.00 x 1.01) = 2.6564 vs 2.69 nominal), so the true worst case is 1.176 x 2.6564 = 3.12 V, not 3.10 V. Also, the 1% tolerance itself is an assumption — no tolerance field is set on R23/R55 anywhere in the schematic. One thing worth adding to the write-up: C41 (15 pF) is the FB2 feed-forward capacitor and is the value LTC's own two-cell 3.3 V typical application specifies for a 1.78M/1.00M divider; changing R23 to 1.69 M shifts the feed-forward zero from 1/(2*pi*1.78M*15p) = 5.96 kHz to 6.28 kHz, which is negligible — I checked, and it is worth saying it was checked.

findings.title: Keep U4 (VAUD) linear — the PSRR is worth far more than the 4 mW it typically costs
findings.current_part: U4 = NCV8164ASN250T1G feeding VAUD = 2.5 V, which supplies U6 LM4853 (VDD), U7 TLV9364 (V+) and U9 SN74LVC2G34 (VCC) — i.e. the power amplifier, the four filter op-amps and the audio buffer, everything in the analogue chain. Verified NCV8164 noise and rejection: PSRR 83 dB at 100 Hz, 85 dB at 1 kHz, 80 dB at 10 kHz, 61 dB at 100 kHz (VOUT(NOM) = 3.3 V, IOUT = 10 mA); output voltage noise 9 uVRMS over 10 Hz to 100 kHz at 10 mA (fixed version). Stable with any ceramic >= 1 uF with no minimum ESR and no stated maximum, so the 13 uF nominal on VAUD is fine.
findings.proposal: Leave U4 exactly as it is. If a switcher goes anywhere in this domain, it goes on VDD2, never on VAUD.
findings.benefit: Sizing the prize honestly, because that is the whole point: MBL annotate '~100mW' beside U4 and state publicly that audio draws 'something like 50 to 100 mW at max volume'. At the worst case, 100 mW / 2.5 V = 40 mA, so U4's loss is 0.836 x 40 = 33.4 mW at the LDO, 36.3 mW referred to the battery. But that is only at maximum volume into the speaker; at the ~5 mA I estimate for idle and normal listening the loss is 0.836 x 5 = 4.2 mW, i.e. 4.5 mW at the battery. Averaged over play the available saving from switching this rail is a few milliwatts, and even the absolute worst case is 36 mW — less than the VDD2 lever, on the rail where noise matters most. Trading 85 dB of 1 kHz rejection and 9 uVRMS of noise for a few milliwatts on a board whose stated selling point is 'crystal clear audio' is a bad trade at any operating point.
findings.risk: The risk is in doing the swap, not in leaving it: no small buck or buck-boost comes near 80-85 dB of in-band rejection, and VAUD feeds the amplifier directly. Note also the corollary that cuts the other way — MBL's own schematic note 'Audio seems to sound best when noise on VDD2 is minimized' says the CORE rail's noise is audible in this design too. That is the strongest single argument against the two switcher proposals above, and it means any VDD2 switcher has to be signed off by listening, not by measuring. If audio quality is the priority over runtime, the correct answer in this domain may be to change nothing at all.
findings.verify_reason: Every stated number verified against the onsemi NCV8164 datasheet (rev.5): PSRR 83 dB at 100 Hz, 85 dB at 1 kHz, 80 dB at 10 kHz, 61 dB at 100 kHz, at the stated conditions VOUT(NOM) = 3.3 V, IOUT = 10 mA; output voltage noise 9 uVRMS over f = 10 Hz to 100 kHz at IOUT = 10 mA, fixed version. Stability: 'The NCV8164 does not require a minimum Equivalent Series Resistance (ESR) for the output capacitor. The device is designed to be stable with standard ceramics capacitors with values of 1 uF or greater' — and no maximum is stated anywhere, so the 13 uF on VAUD is fine, as claimed. The VAUD load list is exactly right — I dumped the net: U4.5 (VO), U6.9 (LM4853 VDD), U7.4 (TLV9364 V+), U9.5 (SN74LVC2G34 VCC), plus C9/C36/C54 at 1u and C59 at 10u = 13 uF nominal, and four 100k. The '~100mW' annotation is real: it sits at (241.3, 138.684) in AGBM-01_AA_1-2.kicad_sch, immediately below the VAUD power flag and TP22 at (241.3, 135.89) — it is annotating the VAUD rail, not something else. Arithmetic redone: 100 mW / 2.5 V = 40 mA; (3.336-2.5) x 40 mA = 33.4 mW at the LDO, /0.92 = 36.3 mW at the battery; at 5 mA, 0.836 x 5 = 4.2 -> 4.5 mW. All reproduce. The finding also does the thing the brief asks for and most findings do not: it sizes its own prize honestly, states that the absolute worst case is 36 mW and the typical case a few mW, and then recommends against taking it. The corollary it draws — that MBL's 'Audio seems to sound best when noise on VDD2 is minimized' note (verified verbatim at 99.06,87.63, directly above U8 at 99.06,100.33) is the strongest argument against the two VDD2 switcher proposals — is a fair and useful cross-reference.
findings.correction: Nothing to correct. Two additions that strengthen it. (1) Independent corroboration I found while checking the other findings: AGBM-02 — the board where MBL had two TPS63802 buck-boosts already on the BOM and could trivially have run one at 2.5 V — still keeps an NCV8164 LDO on VAUD (and on VDD2). The designer had the switcher in hand and chose the linear anyway. That is the strongest available evidence for this recommendation and it should be cited. (2) The one unsourced claim in the finding is 'no small buck or buck-boost comes near 80-85 dB of in-band rejection'. It is directionally right but it is a generic assertion, not a fetched number; since the recommendation is to change nothing, being wrong about it costs nothing, but it should be marked as judgement rather than spec.

findings.title: There is no drop-in LDO upgrade worth having — the best possible same-footprint swap is 0.1 mW
findings.current_part: NCV8164ASN250T1G in TSOP-5: Iq 30 uA typ / 40 uA max at IOUT = 0; shutdown 0.01 uA typ / 1.5 uA max; dropout 125 mV typ / 200 mV max at 300 mA for the 2.5 V option; output accuracy +/-2% over 0.1-300 mA; line regulation 0.5 mV/V; load regulation 2 mV; current limit 350 mA min; 260 Ohm active output discharge (the 'A' suffix).
findings.proposal: Do not bother looking for a better LDO. Any 2.5 V linear regulator fed from 3.336 V is 74.9% efficient by definition — the topology, not the part number, sets the efficiency. The only two parameters a different LDO could improve are quiescent current and dropout, and neither is doing anything here.
findings.benefit: Quiescent current: the theoretical maximum saving from replacing 30 uA of Iq with 0 uA is 30 uA x 3.336 V = 0.10 mW at VOUT3, 0.11 mW at the battery — 0.06% of the 170 mW idle figure. That is rounding error and I am reporting it as rounding error. Dropout: with 0.836 V of headroom and 48 mA of load (implied pass-element drop of ~20 mV typ, ~32 mV max, scaling the 125/200 mV at 300 mA specification), dropout has roughly 25x margin and is irrelevant. Current limit 350 mA minimum against a 48 mA worst-case load is 7x margin. There is nothing left on the table in the same footprint.
findings.risk: None — the risk is spending effort here instead of on the switcher question. Worth stating explicitly because 'find a better LDO' is the natural first move and it is a dead end.
findings.verify_reason: Every parameter cited is in the datasheet and every one is correct: Iq 30 uA typ / 40 uA max at IOUT = 0 mA; shutdown current 0.01 uA typ / 1.5 uA max at VEN <= 0.25 V; dropout 125 mV typ / 200 mV max at IOUT = 300 mA for VOUT(NOM) = 2.5 V; output voltage accuracy +/-2% over 0.1 mA <= IOUT <= 300 mA; line regulation 0.5 mV/V; load regulation 2 mV for IOUT = 1 mA to 300 mA; output current limit 350 mA min (560 mA max) at VOUT = 90% VOUT(NOM); and 'Active output discharge resistance, VEN < 0.25 V, Version A only, RDIS = 260 ohm' — the A-suffix attribution is right, and NCV8164ASN250T1G appears in the ordering table as the 2.5 V TSOP-5 part 'With Active Output Discharge'. Arithmetic redone: 30 uA x 3.336 V = 0.100 mW at VOUT3, /0.92 = 0.109 mW at the battery, which is 0.064% of 170 mW; 2.5/3.336 = 74.94% so the topology claim is exact; scaling the 125/200 mV at 300 mA gives 20 mV typ / 32 mV max at 48 mA, roughly 25x margin; 350 mA / 48 mA = 7.3x. The finding's central argument is also structurally sound: a 2.5 V linear from 3.336 V is fixed at 74.9% by the topology, so the only levers a different LDO offers are Iq and dropout, and both are verified to be irrelevant here. It reports 0.1 mW as rounding error rather than dressing it up, which is exactly what the brief asks for.
findings.correction: One caveat to add for precision: onsemi specifies quiescent current only at IOUT = 0 mA (30 uA typ / 40 uA max) and publishes no ground-current-versus-load figure, so 30 uA is a floor on the LDO's own consumption at 30-48 mA of load, not a measured value at that load. Even if the real ground current were three times the zero-load figure, the theoretical maximum saving from a zero-Iq replacement would still be only ~0.3 mW. The conclusion does not move. Also, the two LDOs together (U8 and U4) put the whole-board figure at ~0.2 mW rather than 0.1 mW, if one wants the board-level number rather than the per-part one.

findings.title: Re-purposing an LTC3527 channel for VDD2 is physically impossible — it is a boost-only topology and VCC is above 2.5 V on fresh cells
findings.current_part: U5 = LTC3527, dual synchronous STEP-UP converter, QFN-16. Channel 1 (VOUT1, FB1 from R21 1.78 M / R22 560 k) makes 1.20 x 4.17857 = 5.014 V for the screen and the cart 5 V pad; channel 2 (VOUT2, FB2 from R23 1.78 M / R55 1.00 M) makes 1.20 x 2.78 = 3.336 V for everything else. Datasheet: output adjustable 1.6 V to 5.25 V, maximum duty cycle clamped at 90% typical, peak inductor current 900 mA (converter 1) / 500 mA (converter 2), input can drop as low as 0.5 V after start-up.
findings.proposal: Rule this out and stop considering it. Both channels are already committed to loads that cannot be dropped (5 V for the screen, 3.3 V for the CPU I/O and cart), and even if a channel were free, a step-up converter cannot produce 2.5 V from a VCC that is 3.2 V on fresh alkalines — it would simply pass VIN through. The minimum programmable output of 1.6 V describes the feedback range, not an ability to buck.
findings.benefit: Zero. Stating this is worth including because 'you already have a dual converter, use the spare channel' is the obvious first idea and it does not work; ruling it out cleanly is what pushes the answer to a third converter (finding vdd2-buckboost-from-vcc) or to a post-boost buck (finding u8-ldo-to-buck-from-vout3).
findings.risk: None. Note the corollary for the buck-boost proposal: because the pack spans 1.8-3.2 V and the target is 2.5 V, the converter must genuinely be buck-boost, not boost — which is why the TPS63900/TPS63802 class is the right one and why the AGBM-02's choice of buck-boost topology is the relevant precedent.
findings.verify_reason: I read the LTC3527 datasheet cover to cover rather than trusting the summary. The 'VIN > VOUT Operation' section is on p.12 under Applications Information and I rendered the page to read the formula exactly (the text layer garbles it): POUT = IOUT[(VIN + 1.5) - VOUT]. Its existence flatly refutes the finding's central technical assertion. Everything else in the finding checks out: U5 is an LTC3527 in a 16-lead 3mm x 3mm QFN (UD package), described on the title page as 'Dual 800mA/400mA, 1.2MHz/2.2MHz Synchronous Step-Up DC/DC Converters'; feedback voltage 1.176/1.20/1.224 V; output voltage adjust range 1.6-5.25 V at 25 C (1.7 V min over the full temperature range) and VOUT = 1.20[1 + R1/R2] from the FB1 pin description; maximum duty cycle 85% min / 90% typ; 'Peak switch current is limited to approximately 900mA for converter 1 and 500mA for converter 2, independent of input or output voltage' (note the guaranteed electrical-table minima are 800 mA and 400 mA); '0.5V to 5V VIN Range After Start-Up'. Divider maths reproduce from the board data: R21 1.78 M / R22 560 k gives 1.20 x 4.17857 = 5.014 V on VOUT5, R23 1.78 M / R55 1.00 M gives 1.20 x 2.78 = 3.336 V on VOUT3 — and the 1.78M/1M pair is literally the divider in LTC's own two-cell-alkaline typical application on the datasheet front page. Both channels' commitments verified from the netlist: VOUT5 feeds U11 (screen/cart 5 V) and U14; VOUT3 feeds U8, U4 and U18. The corollary the finding draws — that a genuine buck-boost is needed because the pack spans 1.8-3.2 V around a 2.5 V target, which is why the TPS63900/TPS63802 class is the right one — is correct and is the useful part of the item. I am marking this REVISED rather than CONFIRMED because a hardware review that tells the reader a part is physically incapable of something its own datasheet documents is exactly the failure mode the brief warns about, even when the bottom-line advice happens to land in the right place.
findings.correction: The recommendation (rule it out) survives; the reason given for it is contradicted by the datasheet and must be replaced. The finding asserts 'a step-up converter cannot produce 2.5 V from a VCC that is 3.2 V on fresh alkalines — it would simply pass VIN through.' The LTC3527 datasheet has a section titled 'VIN > VOUT Operation' which says the opposite: 'The LTC3527/LTC3527-1 will maintain output voltage regulation even when the input voltage is above one or both of the desired output voltages. Note, all VINS must be common to support this mode of operation.' On this board that precondition is met — U5 pads 4 (VIN1), 9 (VIN2) and 15 (VIN) are all on VCC. So the part can regulate below VIN; the claim of physical impossibility is simply wrong. The correct reasons to rule it out are two, and they are both sufficient: (a) both channels are already committed to loads that cannot be dropped and there is no third channel, and (b) even if one were free, the datasheet states this mode 'is less efficient and will dissipate more power', defining POUT = IOUT[(VIN + 1.5) - VOUT] with a thermal budget (POUT1 + POUT2) x 68 C/W = 125 - TA. At VIN = 3.2 V, VOUT = 2.5 V, IOUT = 48 mA that is 0.048 x (4.7 - 2.5) = 106 mW of budgeted dissipation against the 40 mW the LDO burns today. So it is worse than what it would replace — a far stronger argument than the false one the finding makes.

findings.title: U8 is nowhere near thermally limited even at 1.75x — the overclock does not create a reliability problem here, only an efficiency one
findings.current_part: NCV8164 in TSOP-5: thermal resistance junction-to-ambient 158 C/W, junction-to-board 197 C/W, psi-JB 82 C/W; maximum junction temperature 150 C absolute, but onsemi state 'For reliable operation junction temperature should be limited to +125 C'; thermal shutdown at 165 C rising with 15 C hysteresis; PD(MAX) = (TJ(MAX) - TA)/theta-JA. Output short circuit duration is rated unlimited.
findings.proposal: No change. Record the headroom so nobody adds a heatsink, a bigger package (WDFNW6 at 51 C/W or DFNW8 at 50 C/W are both available in 2.5 V as NCV8164AML250TCG) or a thermal via field to solve a problem that does not exist.
findings.benefit: Zero milliwatts, but it settles the question. At TA = 40 C inside a sealed GBA shell, PD(MAX) = (125 - 40)/158 = 538 mW. U8's actual dissipation is 25.2 mW at 1x and 40.2 mW at 1.75x with the 48 mA central estimate (44.4 mW at the top of my 53 mA band). At 40.2 mW the junction rise is 40.2 mW x 158 C/W = 6.4 C, so TJ ~= 46 C. That is 13x margin on power and the current limit (350 mA minimum) is 7x above the 48 mA load. The DFNW8 package would cut the rise to 2.0 C and buy nothing.
findings.risk: None. The one thing this does establish is that if you keep the LDO, you are not risking the part — you are simply choosing to spend 40 mW of battery on heat. That is a legitimate choice on a console whose peak draw is 1175 mW, and it should be framed as a runtime decision rather than a safety one.
findings.verify_reason: All the thermal figures are verbatim from the datasheet's Thermal Characteristics table for the TSOP-5 package: RthetaJA 158 C/W, RthetaJB 197 C/W, psi-JB 82 C/W; and from Absolute Maximum Ratings, TJ 150 C with 'Output Short Circuit Duration, tSC, unlimited'. Thermal shutdown 165 C rising with 15 C hysteresis confirmed in the electrical table. The Applications Information section states verbatim 'For reliable operation junction temperature should be limited to +125 C, however device is capable to work up to junction temperature +150 C' and gives PD(MAX) = (TJ(MAX) - TA)/RthetaJA, so the finding's use of 125 C rather than 150 C is the datasheet's own guidance, not a made-up derate. WDFNW6 51 C/W and DFNW8 50 C/W are both correct as package numbers. Arithmetic redone and it all reproduces: (125-40)/158 = 538 mW; (3.336-2.5) x 30 mA = 25.1 mW at 1x and x 48 mA = 40.1 mW at 1.75x (44.3 mW at 53 mA); 40.2 mW x 158 C/W = 6.35 C rise so TJ ~46 C at TA = 40 C; 538/40.2 = 13.4x; 350 mA / 48 mA = 7.3x; 40.2 mW x 50 C/W = 2.0 C for DFNW8. The framing at the end — that keeping the LDO is a runtime decision rather than a safety one, spending ~40 mW of battery on heat in a console whose peak is 1175 mW — is accurate and useful. I am marking REVISED rather than CONFIRMED only because a stated part-availability claim is verifiably false against the ordering table; the engineering conclusion is untouched.
findings.correction: The substance is right — U8 has ~13x power margin and ~7x current-limit margin, and nobody should add cooling. One factual error in the parenthetical: 'WDFNW6 at 51 C/W or DFNW8 at 50 C/W are both available in 2.5 V as NCV8164AML250TCG' is wrong twice over. Per the ordering table on p.10, the WDFNW6 package is offered only in ADJ, 1.1 V, 1.2 V, 1.8 V, 2.8 V and 2.9 V — there is no 2.5 V WDFNW6 part at all. And NCV8164AML250TCG is the DFNW8 device (marking KP), not the WDFNW6; the WDFNW6 parts carry the AMTW prefix. So the only lower-theta 2.5 V option is DFNW8 at 50 C/W, which as the finding correctly computes would cut a 6.4 C rise to 2.0 C and buy nothing.

findings.title: U8 and U4 are drawn with a schematic symbol named MCP1824 while their Value is NCV8164ASN250T1G — the board is right, the library is misleading
findings.current_part: In AGBM-01_AA_1-2.kicad_sch both U8 (at 99.06, 100.33) and U4 (at 222.25, 135.89) are instantiated with lib_id 'OpenGBA:MCP1824', while their Value property and the PCB footprint value are 'NCV8164ASN250T1G' in a Bucketmouse:SOT-23-5 footprint. The MCP1824 is a different manufacturer's part; the symbol is being reused for pin compatibility.
findings.proposal: Rename the symbol (or re-point it at a proper NCV8164 symbol) so the library and the BOM agree. No electrical change. I verified the electrical part before flagging it: the instantiated pin numbering is 1 = VOUT3, 2 = GND, 3 = enable input, 4 = PG, 5 = output, which matches the NCV8164 pin function table for TSOP-5 exactly ('1 IN / 2 GND / 3 EN / 5 OUT' with 'PG' on pin 4). The board is correct as manufactured.
findings.benefit: Zero milliwatts. The value is in avoiding a wrong order: anyone regenerating a BOM from the symbol library rather than from the Value field, or substituting the 'real' symbol from a vendor library, could get a different pinout convention and would not find out until the LDO is dead on the bench. On a board where U8 feeds a salvaged, irreplaceable CPU, that is worth the five minutes.
findings.risk: None from fixing it. I am deliberately not asserting anything about the actual MCP1824's pinout, because I did not fetch its datasheet — the verified claim here is only that the instantiated pin numbers match the NCV8164, so the fabricated board is correct.
findings.verify_reason: Verified directly in AGBM-01_AA_1-2.kicad_sch. Both instances carry (lib_id "OpenGBA:MCP1824") with (property "Value" "NCV8164ASN250T1G") and (property "Footprint" "Bucketmouse:SOT-23-5"); U8 is at (at 99.06 100.33 0) and U4 at (at 222.25 135.89 ...), exactly the coordinates the finding gives. I also pulled the symbol definition itself from the embedded library block: its pins are 1 = VI (power_in), 2 = GND (power_in), 3 = ~SHDN (power_out), 4 = PGOOD (open_collector), 5 = VO (power_out). Against the NCV8164 pin function table for TSOP-5 — 1 IN, 2 GND, 3 EN, 4 PG, 5 OUT — the pin NUMBERS match one for one, so the finding's core claim that the board as manufactured is correct is verified, and its own pad-net reading (1 = VOUT3, 2 = GND, 3 = enable, 4 = PG, 5 = output) matches the fork's netlist for both parts. The finding is also disciplined in the right way: it explicitly declines to assert anything about the real MCP1824's pinout because it did not fetch that datasheet, and scopes its claim to what it verified. That is the correct handling. Zero mW, correctness category, and the failure mode it guards against — someone regenerating a BOM from the symbol library or substituting a vendor MCP1824 symbol and getting a different pinout convention on a rail feeding an irreplaceable salvaged CPU — is real.
findings.correction: Correct as written, and it can be made stronger. The mismatch is not only the part name — the symbol also mislabels the enable polarity. The OpenGBA:MCP1824 symbol defines pin 3 as '~SHDN' (an active-LOW shutdown, and typed 'power_out', which is itself an odd electrical type for an input), whereas the NCV8164's pin 3 is an active-HIGH enable: 'Applying VEN < 0.25 V disables the regulator, Pulling VEN > 0.7 V enables the LDO'. The board's wiring is right for an active-high enable — /PG_3V3 into U8 and /PG_2V5 into U4, both open-collector-high-when-good with pull-ups — so the fabricated board is correct as the finding says, but anyone reading the schematic off the symbol's pin labels would conclude the enable polarity is inverted from what the fitted part actually does. That is a sharper version of the same hazard the finding identifies and worth folding into the write-up.

findings.title: Both PCB footprints carry a stale Value "0467001.NR" — a 0603 1 A fuse in an 0805 land, which would delete the resettable protection entirely
findings.current_part: Three part numbers are in play. (1) Schematic Value: F1 = F0805B2R00FSTR, PTC1 = 0805L075SLYR. (2) PCB footprint Value on BOTH F1 and PTC1 = 0467001.NR. (3) KiCad Description field on both = 0805L050WR. Verified identities: 0467001.NR is a Littelfuse 467 Series fuse — the datasheet's own title page reads "467 Series / 0603 Fast-Acting Fuse", and the 1.00 A row gives 32 V, nominal cold resistance 0.0700 ohm, nominal melting I2t 0.0212 A2s. It is a 0603 part and a one-shot fuse, not a PPTC. 0805L050WR is a standard (non-LoRho) 0805L PPTC, 0.50 A hold / 1.00 A trip, R_min 0.150 / R_1max 0.850 ohm — the ordering-code table in the 0805L datasheet lists "0805L050WR" as the orderable code for 0805L050. Footprint on the board is Bucketmouse:Fuse_0805_2012Metric, pads 0.975 x 1.4 mm at 1.875 mm pitch.
findings.proposal: The SCHEMATIC is authoritative; re-sync the PCB Value fields. Two independent pieces of evidence settle it. (a) Package: 0467001.NR is a 0603 body (2.0 x 1.25 mm nominal land is not it — the 467 datasheet is titled "0603 Fast-Acting Fuse"), and both board footprints are 0805 lands; the schematic values F0805B2R00FSTR and 0805L075SLYR are both genuine 0805 parts. (b) Cross-design: I checked MouseBiteLabs' own AGBM-02, which is the later derivative of this board — its PCB footprints carry F1 = "F0805B2R00FSTR" and PTC1 = "0805L075SLYR", matching its schematic. Only AGBM-01 rev 1.2's PCB has the 0467001.NR strings, in both slots. That is a classic un-synced "Update PCB from Schematic" with "replace values" left off, and it was fixed by the time AGBM-02 shipped. The "0805L050WR" Description is a third artifact — it is present on F1 AND PTC1 in AGBM-01, AGBM-02 and AGBM-11 alike, i.e. a legacy string baked into the library symbol, not a BOM entry. Action: open the PCB, set F1 Value = F0805B2R00FSTR and PTC1 Value = 0805L075SLYR (or the 0805L150SLYR from the next finding), and clear/repair the Description on both. No copper, no land pattern, no schematic change.
findings.benefit: This is a build-correctness fix, not a power saving, but it has a quantifiable failure cost. If anyone exports a BOM from the layout (which is what a fab/JLCPCB BOM+CPL flow typically does) they would stuff two 0467001.NR: 2 x 0.0700 ohm = 0.140 ohm total. Loss at 292 mA = 0.292^2 x 0.140 = 11.9 mW; at 390 mA = 21.3 mW; at 750 mA = 78.8 mW. That is worse than the correct build's best case (0.120 ohm) and, far more importantly, there is then NO resettable device on the board — every overcurrent event becomes a permanent fuse replacement. On top of that a 1 A fuse is marginal for the load: at the 750 mA overclocked peak it runs at 75% of rating, and the 467 series' own opening-time table specifies only "4 hours minimum" at 100% of rating, with an operating range to +90 C; derated for a sealed GBA shell it will nuisance-blow. And mechanically a 0603 body on an 0805 land is a self-alignment/tombstone hazard.
findings.risk: None to the fix itself — it is a metadata edit. The risk is in NOT fixing it: an automated BOM export produces a board that is both lossier and unprotected, and the builder has no way to tell from the layout that the schematic disagrees.
findings.verify_reason: I reproduced every claim independently. (a) Parsed both PCBs with my own s-expression parser: AGBM-01 rev1.2 and the fork carry F1 Value='0467001.NR' and PTC1 Value='0467001.NR', while the AGBM-01 schematic carries F1='F0805B2R00FSTR', PTC1='0805L075SLYR'. AGBM-02's PCB carries the correct values matching its schematic. Confirmed. (b) I went further and diffed EVERY schematic-vs-PCB Value in AGBM-01: exactly 6 mismatches — F1, PTC1, R3 (5.1k sch / 1k pcb), R4 (33k/10k), R64 (200k/100k), TP22 (BATT/VAUD). That is decisive evidence for the un-synced 'Update PCB from Schematic' diagnosis, and it is a stronger finding than the one written: a layout-derived BOM would also mis-stuff R3/R4/R64. (c) Littelfuse 467 datasheet extracted with pypdf: title 'Fuse Datasheet ... 0603 Fast-Acting Fuse'; 1.00 A row = 32 V, nominal cold resistance 0.0700 ohm, nominal melting I2t 0.0212 A2sec, nominal Vdrop 67.40 mV, nominal Pd 0.0674 W; notes '1. Measured at 10% of rated current, 25C'; opening time table '100% => 4 hours minimum, 200% => 5 s max, 300% => 0.2 s max'. All as stated. (d) 0805L standard datasheet: 0805L050 = Ihold 0.50, Itrip 1.00, Vmax 6, Imax 100, Rmin 0.150, R1max 0.850, and '0805L050WR' IS a listed orderable code — so the Description string is a stale library artifact as claimed. (e) Footprint pads read from the .kicad_pcb: F1 and PTC1 both 0.975 x 1.4 mm at +/-0.9375 (1.875 mm pitch), Fuse_0805_2012Metric. Arithmetic redone: 2 x 0.0700 = 0.140 ohm; 0.292^2 x 0.140 = 11.94 mW, 0.390^2 x 0.140 = 21.3 mW, 0.750^2 x 0.140 = 78.8 mW. All correct. Two small corrections that do not change anything: the correct build's worst case is 0.080 + 0.150 = 0.230 ohm, not 0.240 (see the R1max correction in the next finding); and the '0805L050WR Description present on F1 AND PTC1 in AGBM-11' is only half true — AGBM-11's F1 Description is 'Fuse'/empty, only its PTC1 carries the string. The metadata-only fix is correct and zero-risk.
findings.correction: Widen the fix: four more PCB Values are stale in AGBM-01 (R3 5.1k->1k, R4 33k->10k, R64 200k->100k, TP22 BATT->VAUD), so re-sync the whole board, not just F1/PTC1. Correct-build series resistance range is 0.120-0.230 ohm (not 0.120-0.240).

findings.title: PTC1: swap 0805L075SLYR for 0805L150SLYR — same series, same 0805 land, R_1max drops 160 mohm to 65 mohm
findings.current_part: PTC1 = Littelfuse 0805L075SLYR, PolySwitch LoRho series, 0805 (2012 metric). Verified from the LoRho datasheet table: I_hold 0.75 A, I_trip 1.50 A, V_max 6 Vdc, I_max 50 A, P_d 0.6 W, max time-to-trip 0.20 s at 8.00 A, R_min 0.040 ohm, R_1max 0.160 ohm. Newark confirms 750 mA / 1.5 A / 6 VDC / 50 A / 0805 / "PolySwitch Low Rho Series"; LCSC's parametric page independently lists R min 40 mohm (it lists R1 max as 150 mohm, 10 mohm below the datasheet — I use the datasheet's 160 mohm). Netlist position: PTC1.1 = VBATT, PTC1.2 = VCC, and VCC goes only to U5 VIN/VIN1/VIN2, L1, L2 and C37 — so 100% of the converter's input current passes through it.
findings.proposal: Littelfuse 0805L150SLYR, same LoRho series, same 0805 land pattern, same 6 V / 50 A ratings. Verified: I_hold 1.50 A, I_trip 3.00 A, V_max 6 Vdc, I_max 50 A, R_min 0.015 ohm, R_1max 0.065 ohm, time to trip 500 ms (DigiKey and LCSC parametric pages both give Ri min 15 mohm / R1 max 65 mohm, and the LoRho datasheet table gives the same). Sourcing: DigiKey 13,328 in stock at $2.26/1 down to $0.80/4000; LCSC 4,575 in stock at $0.343 at qty 5. Second source with identical numbers if wanted: Bourns MF-PSML150 (0805, R_min 0.015 / R_1max 0.065, I_hold 1.50 / I_trip 3.00) — note that specific MF-PSML part is marked obsolete by Bourns in favour of the MF-PSML/X generation, so the Littelfuse part is the cleaner choice.
findings.benefit:
Delta R = 0.040 - 0.015 = 0.025 ohm on a fresh part, or 0.160 - 0.065 = 0.095 ohm post-reflow (R_1max is defined as the resistance one hour after tripping or after 260 C/20 s reflow, so a built board sits nearer the R_1max end). Mid-estimate delta R = 0.060 ohm. Saving = I^2 x dR:
  200 mA:  1.0 / 3.8 mW (mid 2.4)
  292 mA (700 mW at 2.4 V):  2.1 / 8.1 mW (mid 5.1)
  350 mA:  3.1 / 11.6 mW (mid 7.4)
  390 mA (935 mW overclocked at 2.4 V):  3.8 / 14.5 mW (mid 9.1)
  550 mA:  7.6 / 28.7 mW (mid 18.2)
  750 mA (overclocked, low battery):  14.1 / 53.4 mW (mid 33.8)
As a fraction of the console: 0.7-1.2% of a 700 mW draw, 2.4-4.5% of the 1410 mW overclocked worst case. At the 170 mW idle point (71 mA at 2.4 V) the saving is 0.13-0.48 mW, i.e. genuinely nothing — this lever only pays under load, and I am not going to pretend otherwise.
Secondary benefit that is not power: converter input droop. At 750 mA the stock pair drops 90-180 mV; with 0805L150SLYR + the stock fuse it drops 60-110 mV. That is 30-70 mV of extra headroom before the low-battery supervisor cuts out. Do not overclaim runtime from this: the cells' own 300-600 mohm ESR contributes 225-450 mV of the sag at the same current, so the board is only ~25% of the total droop, and how that converts to minutes depends on the cell discharge curve, which I have not verified.
findings.risk: I_trip rises from 1.50 A to 3.00 A, so the resettable device becomes less sensitive. In practice this changes little, because F1 already wins every fast fault (see the f1-redundant-lower-r finding): F1's pre-arc I2t is 0.030 A2s, so at a battery-limited 5 A fault it opens in ~1.2 ms while even the 0.75 A PPTC's datasheet max time-to-trip is 0.20 s at 8 A. The PPTC's unique coverage is slow overloads, and that band shifts from 1.5-4 A to 3-4 A. Given the pack's 300-600 mohm ESR limits the available fault current to roughly 3-8 A at 3 V, a 3 A trip point is still reachable. Cost delta is about $0.05 at LCSC quantities. No footprint, schematic or layout change.
findings.verify_reason: The part and the direction are real; one key number is wrong and the risk section's justification is unsupported. VERIFIED: I pulled the Littelfuse Low Rho datasheet (Rev GD 03/06/25) and extracted the electrical table with pypdf. Row '0805L150SL -K 1.50 3.00 6 50 0.6 8.00 0.50 0.015 0.065' — Ihold 1.50 A, Itrip 3.00 A, Vmax 6 Vdc, Imax 50 A, Pd 0.6 W, max time-to-trip 0.50 s at 8.00 A, Rmin 0.015, R1max 0.065. Exactly as claimed. The ordering table lists 0805L150SLYR (4,000/reel). DigiKey shows it Active, 13,328 in stock, $2.26/1 down to $0.80/4000, 0805 (2012 Metric). Drop-in on the existing Fuse_0805_2012Metric land (0.975 x 1.4 pads, 1.875 mm pitch) — confirmed. Netlist position confirmed: PTC1.1=VBATT, PTC1.2=VCC, and VCC carries only C37, L1, L2, TP32 and U5 VIN/VIN1/VIN2, so 100% of converter input current passes through it. WRONG: the stock part's R1max is 0.150 ohm, not 0.160. The same datasheet row reads '0805L075SL -G 0.75 1.50 6 50 0.6 8.00 0.20 0.040 0.150'. The finding saw LCSC's 150 mohm, called it '10 mohm below the datasheet' and overrode it with 0.160 — it had the correct value in hand and discarded it. So dR post-reflow is 0.150-0.065 = 0.085, not 0.095; mid-estimate 0.055, not 0.060. Recomputed I^2 x dR (min/max, mid): 200 mA 1.0/3.4 (2.2); 292 mA 2.1/7.3 (4.7); 350 mA 3.1/10.4 (6.7); 390 mA 3.8/12.9 (8.4); 550 mA 7.6/25.7 (16.6); 750 mA 14.1/47.8 (30.9). Roughly 8-10% less than claimed at every point. ALSO WRONG: the risk section dismisses the 1.5 A -> 3.0 A trip increase on the grounds that 'F1 opens in ~1.2 ms into a 5 A fault ... roughly 400x' faster than the PPTC. That extrapolation is invalid. The Accu-Guard II datasheet specifies pre-arc I2t = 0.030 A2sec AT 50 A (column header: 'Pre-Arc I2t @ 50A'), and the same datasheet carries explicit 'FUSE PRE-ARC JOULE INTEGRALS VS CURRENT' curves plotted from 0 to 60 A precisely because I2t is strongly current-dependent below the adiabatic region. The tabulated 'Fusing Current (within 5 sec), 25C = 4.00 A' means the 2 A element takes up to 5 SECONDS at 4 A. At the pack-limited 3-8 A fault current the fuse is in the 0.1-5 s range, i.e. comparable to or slower than the PPTC's 0.20 s max at 8 A.
