F1 does not win every race, so raising Itrip from 1.5 A to 3.0 A is a genuine reduction in coverage: a sustained 1.5-3 A overload would then trip nothing (it is also below the 2 A fuse's rating). The efficiency case survives; the 'protection unchanged' case does not.
findings.correction: Stock 0805L075SLYR R1max = 0.150 ohm (not 0.160). dR = 0.025 (fresh) to 0.085 (post-reflow), mid 0.055. Saving: 4.7 mW at 292 mA (was 5.1), 8.4 mW at 390 mA (was 9.1), 30.9 mW at 750 mA (was 33.8), 0.13-0.43 mW at the 71 mA idle point. Input droop at 750 mA: stock 90-173 mV, upgraded 71-109 mV. And the risk must be restated honestly: the 1.5->3.0 A trip increase leaves the 1.5-3 A sustained-overload band covered by nothing, because F1 at 4 A takes up to 5 s per its own table.

findings.title: PTC1's derated hold current is below the ClockxControl peak input current — the console can latch off at max brightness on a half-flat pack
findings.current_part: 0805L075SLYR, I_hold 0.75 A specified in 20 C still air. Littelfuse's own LoRho temperature-rerating table for this exact part number: -40 C 1.24 A, -20 C 1.07, 0 C 0.94, 20 C 0.75, 40 C 0.62, 60 C 0.47, 70 C 0.37, 85 C 0.23. I_trip at 20 C is 1.50 A, so between 0.75 A and 1.50 A the device is in its indeterminate band: it does not reliably hold and does not reliably trip, it just heats and its resistance climbs.
findings.proposal: Same swap as ptc1-lorho-075-to-150: 0805L150SLYR. Its rerating table (same datasheet, same units): -40 C 2.37 A, 20 C 1.50, 40 C 1.25, 60 C 0.93, 70 C 0.74, 85 C 0.50. At any plausible internal temperature it holds the overclocked peak with margin.
findings.benefit:
Arithmetic for the peak input current. Measured max in-use is 1175 mW (Hispeedido IPS at max brightness, Everdrive, max volume, speaker). The ClockxControl adds 150-240 mW at the battery (see measured_anchors; I use +235 mW), giving ~1410 mW. Input current = 1410 mW / V_pack: 588 mA at 2.4 V, 705 mA at 2.0 V, 783 mA at 1.8 V. So the overclocked peak is 0.59-0.78 A.
Against the fitted part: I_hold is 0.75 A only at 20 C. A GBA shell is sealed with no ventilation and is dissipating ~1.4 W; a 15-25 C internal rise over a 22 C room puts PTC1 at 37-47 C, where interpolating the Littelfuse table gives I_hold = 0.62-0.67 A. The peak draw of 0.70-0.78 A therefore exceeds I_hold at any realistic internal temperature, and sits inside the 0.75-1.50 A hold/trip band. Two consequences: (1) the device self-heats and its resistance rises well above the 0.160 ohm R_1max figure, so the losses in the previous finding are lower bounds precisely when the current is highest; (2) it can latch, which on this board means the console dies mid-game and stays dead until the PPTC cools.
With 0805L150SLYR: I_hold at 40 C is 1.25 A and at 60 C is 0.93 A, both comfortably above 0.78 A. The nuisance-trip mode is removed and the resistance stays in its linear region.
Note this is a marginal call WITHOUT the overclock too: stock peak is 490-653 mA against a 0.62-0.67 A derated hold current. The overclock is what turns a marginal design into a failing one.
findings.risk: The failure mode is not gradual — a PPTC latch is a hard shutdown. Also note the fix is the same single part swap as the efficiency finding, so it is free once you do that one. Residual risk after the swap: I_trip 3.0 A, discussed in the other finding. One caveat I cannot verify: I have no measured internal-ambient figure for this specific shell/screen combination, so the 37-47 C band is an engineering estimate, not a measurement. If the reviewer can measure the temperature at PTC1 under load, the Littelfuse table converts it directly into a hold current.
findings.verify_reason: The conclusion is right and is in fact UNDERSTATED, but the entire derating table quoted is from the wrong part. I extracted the Low Rho datasheet's 'Ambient Operation Temperature / Hold Current (A)' table. The real 0805L075SL row is: -40C 1.15, -20C 1.00, 0C 0.85, 20C 0.75, 40C 0.55, 60C 0.40, 70C 0.30, 85C 0.20. The finding quotes 1.24 / 1.07 / 0.94 / 0.75 / 0.62 / 0.47 / 0.37 / 0.23 — that is the 0603L075SL row (datasheet: 1.23, 1.08, 0.94, 0.75, 0.61, 0.45, 0.36, 0.23). Same mistake on the replacement: it quotes 2.37 / 1.50 / 1.25 / 0.93 / 0.74 / 0.50, which tracks the 0603L150SL row (2.40, 2.10, 1.80, 1.50, 1.25, 0.95, 0.80, 0.50); the real 0805L150SL row is 2.25 / 2.00 / 1.75 / 1.50 / 1.15 / 0.85 / 0.65 / 0.45. The engineer read one package size up the table. Correcting it: interpolating the real 0805L075SL row, Ihold at 37C = 0.58 A and at 47C = 0.50 A, not 0.62-0.67 A. So the stock part is worse than the finding says. SECOND CORRECTION, in the other direction: the 783 mA figure at a 1.8 V pack is not reachable in service. U3 = TPS3840DL20 (2.0 V fixed threshold, 350 nA typ Iq) sits on /VFILT, which is VBATT peak-held by D2 + C1 22u + R9 100k, and its ~RESET drives /EN = LTC3527 SHDN2. The console shuts down at a ~2.0 V pack. Also the ClockxControl adder of +235 mW is the high end: insideGadgets' 12 mA + 40-60 mA gives 173 mW if measured at the battery and ~265 mW if it is 3.3 V rail current reflected through the boost — the finding picked 235 mW without flagging the ambiguity the context file explicitly asks about. Recomputing: total 1325-1440 mW; at 2.4 V that is 552-600 mA, at the 2.0 V cutoff 663-720 mA. So the overclocked peak band is ~0.55-0.72 A, not 0.59-0.78 A. Against the corrected Ihold of 0.50-0.58 A at 37-47C, the peak still exceeds hold across the whole band, and the stock case (490-588 mA) is also over it at the top. Conclusion stands. With 0805L150SLYR the real margins are Ihold 1.15 A at 40C and 0.85 A at 60C against a 0.72 A peak — 1.2x to 1.6x, adequate but tighter than the finding's 0.93 A at 60C implies.
findings.correction: Replace the derating tables with the actual 0805 rows. 0805L075SL: -40C 1.15, -20C 1.00, 0C 0.85, 20C 0.75, 40C 0.55, 60C 0.40, 70C 0.30, 85C 0.20 => Ihold 0.50-0.58 A at a 37-47C internal ambient. 0805L150SL: -40C 2.25, -20C 2.00, 0C 1.75, 20C 1.50, 40C 1.15, 60C 0.85, 70C 0.65, 85C 0.45. Cap the peak input current at ~0.72 A (the TPS3840DL20 2.0 V supervisor cuts the console off before the pack reaches 1.8 V), and state the ClockxControl adder as a 150-265 mW range, not 235 mW.

findings.title: F1 is 0.080 ohm of nearly-redundant series resistance: it wins every fault race against PTC1, and its unique coverage is only the VBATT node
findings.current_part: F1 = F0805B2R00FSTR, Kyocera AVX Accu-Guard II, 0805. Verified from the Accu-Guard II datasheet table (row F0805B2R00FW/STR): 2.00 A rating, resistance 0.080 ohm max measured at 10% of rated current at 25 C, voltage drop 220 mV max at 1 x rated current, fusing current within 5 s = 4.00 A, pre-arc I2t = 0.030 A2sec at 50 A, 63 V rated, 50 A interrupting. The Multicomp MCF0805B2R00FSTR datasheet carries the identical row, cross-validating it. Netlist: F1.1 = Net-(BT1-+), F1.2 = VBATT; PTC1.1 = VBATT, PTC1.2 = VCC. So F1 and PTC1 are in series, and the only nodes between them are D2 (anode), R9, SW1 pin 1 and TP19.
findings.proposal:
Three options, in increasing aggression.
(a) Leave F1 as-is. It costs 0.080 ohm; that is the price of a permanent last-resort disconnect.
(b) F0805B2R50FSTR (0.060 ohm max, 220 mV, fusing current within 5 s = 5.00 A, pre-arc I2t 0.050 A2s, 63 V) or F0805B3R00FSTR (0.050 ohm max, 220 mV, 6.00 A / 5 s, I2t 0.10 A2s, 63 V). Same Accu-Guard II series, same 0805 land, drop-in. A 2 x AA pack at 300-600 mohm ESR can deliver roughly 3-8 A into a dead short at 3 V, so a 2.5 A or 3 A element still opens on a real short.
(c) Build option: fit a 0 ohm 0805 jumper in F1 and rely on PTC1 alone. Zero PCB or schematic change; it is a stuffing choice.
findings.benefit:
Saving = I^2 x dR.
  F1 2 A -> 2.5 A, dR = 0.020 ohm:  0.8 mW at 200 mA, 1.7 at 292, 2.5 at 350, 3.0 at 390, 6.1 at 550, 11.3 at 750 mA.
  F1 2 A -> 3 A, dR = 0.030 ohm:  1.2 / 2.6 / 3.7 / 4.6 / 9.1 / 16.9 mW at the same points.
  F1 -> 0 ohm jumper, dR = 0.080 ohm:  3.2 / 6.8 / 9.8 / 12.2 / 24.2 / 45.0 mW.
Combined with the PTC1 swap (0805L150SLYR + F0805B3R00FSTR): total R falls from 0.120-0.240 ohm to 0.065-0.115 ohm, dR = 0.055-0.125 ohm, worth 4.7-10.7 mW at 292 mA, 8.4-19.0 mW at 390 mA, 16.6-37.8 mW at 550 mA and 30.9-70.3 mW at 750 mA.
Why this is defensible protection-wise: F1 and PTC1 in series is unusual, and F1 always wins the race. F1's pre-arc I2t of 0.030 A2s puts its opening time at 1.2 ms into a 5 A fault and 0.47 ms into 8 A, whereas PTC1's datasheet maximum time-to-trip is 0.20 s at 8 A — roughly 400x slower. So for any hard short the non-resettable device is the one that acts, and the PPTC's resettability is already defeated. Reading the netlist, F1's ONLY unique coverage is a fault on the VBATT node itself: D2 (a 1SS355VM to VFILT), R9 (100k), SW1 pin 1, C1 (22 uF on VFILT) and U3 (TPS3840DL20). Everything else on the board sits behind PTC1. So option (c) gives up protection against a shorted C1 or a shorted D2/U3 — a small, real, but narrow exposure.
findings.risk: Option (b) raises the fuse rating; with a 2 x AA pack whose ESR is 300-600 mohm, the available short-circuit current at 3 V is ~3-8 A, so a 3 A element (6 A / 5 s) is at the edge — I would take the 2.5 A part (5 A / 5 s) rather than the 3 A part for that reason, giving up 1.5 mW at 292 mA to keep the margin. Option (c) removes the only permanent disconnect on the board and leaves the always-on VBATT rail (D2/R9/C1/U3, which are live even with SW1 off) unprotected; I would only do that on a build the owner maintains. Note the 0.080 ohm figure is measured at 10% of rating (200 mA); using the 220 mV / 2 A spec the hot resistance is 0.110 ohm, implying +0.069 ohm/W of self-heating, so at 750 mA (45 mW dissipated) the rise is only ~3 mohm and the cold figure is a good model across the whole range.
findings.verify_reason: The part data and the resistance arithmetic are exactly right; the protection argument that justifies down-rating or removing F1 is not. VERIFIED from the Accu-Guard II datasheet (extracted with pypdf), column headers 'Current Rating A | Resistance 10% x I rated, 25C, ohm (max.) | Voltage Drop @1 x I rated, 25C, mV (max.) | Fusing Current (within 5 sec), 25C, A | Pre-Arc I2t @ 50A, A2-sec | Rated Voltage V', plus 'Interrupting rating: 50A': F0805B2R00FW/STR 2.00 / 0.080 / 220 / 4.00 / 0.030 / 63; F0805B2R50FW/STR 2.50 / 0.060 / 220 / 5.00 / 0.050 / 63; F0805B3R00FW/STR 3.00 / 0.050 / 220 / 6.00 / 0.10 / 63. Every figure the finding cites is correct, and both proposed substitutes exist in the same series and land pattern. Netlist verified: Net-(BT1-+) has exactly three pads — BT1.1 (+), D1.1 (K), F1.1 — and VBATT has D2.2, F1.2, PTC1.1, R9.1, SW1.1, TP19. So F1's unique coverage really is only the VBATT node, as claimed. I redid every I^2 x dR line and they are all correct (0.292^2 x 0.020 = 1.71 mW; 0.750^2 x 0.080 = 45.0 mW; etc.), as is the self-heating check (0.220 V / 2 A = 0.110 ohm hot vs 0.080 cold => 0.068 ohm/W; 45 mW at 750 mA => +3 mohm). REFUTED PART: 'F1's pre-arc I2t of 0.030 A2s puts its opening time at 1.2 ms into a 5 A fault and 0.47 ms into 8 A, whereas PTC1's max time-to-trip is 0.20 s at 8 A - roughly 400x slower.' The 0.030 A2sec is specified AT 50 A, and the datasheet contains dedicated 'PRE-ARC JOULE INTEGRALS VS CURRENT' plots (x-axis 0-60 A) for exactly this reason. The same table says the 2 A element needs up to 5 SECONDS at 4 A. A 2xAA pack at 0.3-0.6 ohm ESR delivers roughly 3-8 A into a dead short, which is in the fuse's slow region, so F1 does not 'always win the race' and the PPTC's 0.20 s at 8 A may well be the faster device. That removes the basis for treating F1 as redundant. Option (c) (0 ohm jumper) should therefore be dropped from the recommendation rather than merely caveated; option (b) at 2.5 A is defensible but buys 1.7 mW at 292 mA, which is rounding error. Combined-swap range also shifts with the corrected R1max: total 0.120-0.230 -> 0.065-0.115 ohm, dR 0.055-0.115 (not 0.055-0.125), worth 4.7-9.8 mW at 292 mA, 8.4-17.5 at 390 mA and 30.9-64.7 at 750 mA.
findings.correction: Keep option (b) at 2.5 A only (1.7 mW at 292 mA, 3.0 mW at 390 mA, 11.3 mW at 750 mA). Withdraw the 'F1 wins every fault race' rationale and with it option (c): the 0.030 A2sec figure is a 50 A specification and cannot be extrapolated to a 3-8 A battery-limited fault, where the datasheet's own 4 A/5 s point governs. Combined dR with the PTC swap is 0.055-0.115 ohm, not 0.055-0.125.

findings.title: D1 is not a Schottky, is 7-13x under-rated for the job, and sits on the wrong side of F1 so its fault current bypasses the fuse entirely
findings.current_part: D1 = ROHM 1SS355VMTE-17, SOD-323F land. The KiCad Description on both D1 and D2 reads "Schottky diode" — that is WRONG. The ROHM datasheet is titled "1SS355VM Switching Diode (High speed switching)", structure "Epitaxial planar", i.e. a silicon small-signal switching diode. Ratings: VR 80 V, VRM 90 V, Io (average rectified forward current) 100 mA, IFM 225 mA, IFSM 500 mA at t = 1 s, VF 1.2 V max at IF = 100 mA, IR 100 nA max at VR = 80 V, trr 4 ns, Ct 3.0 pF. Topology from the netlist: D1.1 (K) = Net-(BT1-+), D1.2 (A) = GND. F1.1 = Net-(BT1-+), F1.2 = VBATT. So D1 and F1 hang off the SAME node — D1 is upstream of the fuse.
findings.proposal: Minimum fix, and it is nearly free: move D1's cathode from Net-(BT1-+) to VBATT, i.e. put the clamp on the load side of F1. That is the textbook shunt-clamp-plus-series-fuse arrangement and it is a schematic net change plus a short trace edit (D1 pad 1 is at (29.40, -28.99), F1 pad 2 / the VBATT F.Cu pour is at (30.26, -24.20) — 4.9 mm away, and the VBATT pour already reaches within about 2 mm of D1). Optional second step if you want the clamp to survive: the SOD-323F land accepts a standard SOD-323 body, and a 1N5819WS / B5819WS class Schottky is 40 V, 1.0 A average, IFSM 25 A at 8.3 ms — enough surge to hold the fault while F1 opens. Before committing to that, VERIFY the reverse leakage at 3 V: the Diodes Inc 1N5817-1N5819 datasheet specifies peak reverse leakage of 1.0 mA at 25 C and 10 mA at 100 C at rated blocking voltage, versus 100 nA max for the 1SS355VM. D1 is permanently across the pack even with SW1 off, so a leaky part is a permanent parasitic drain — this is exactly why you should NOT naively 'upgrade' D1 to a Schottky, and why the KiCad Description being wrong matters.
findings.benefit: No power saving; this is a correctness finding. The failure analysis: with both cells reversed, Net-(BT1-+) sits at roughly -3 V, D1's anode is at GND and its cathode at -3 V, so it is forward-biased directly across the pack. Current is limited only by cell ESR: (3.0 V - ~1.0 V forward drop) / (0.30 to 0.60 ohm) = 3.3 to 6.7 A, call it ~4.4 A at the mid ESR. That is 7-13x D1's IFSM of 500 mA (and that 500 mA is itself a 1-second rating), and ~5 W in a SOD-323FL body. D1 is destroyed in milliseconds. Because D1 and F1 share the BT1+ node, that current NEVER passes through F1, so the fuse does not open and the fault is not cleared — if D1 fails short, the pack stays shorted through a dead diode until the cells vent or drain. Moving D1 to VBATT routes the same current through F1, whose pre-arc I2t of 0.030 A2s corresponds to ~1.6 ms at 4.4 A (and whose specified fusing current within 5 s is 4.00 A), so the fault is cleared. Separately, U5's absolute maximum on VIN/VIN1/VIN2 is -0.3 V to 6 V per the LTC3527 datasheet, and under reverse insertion VCC sits at about -3 V, violating it by 2.7 V — a second reason to want the fault cleared quickly.
findings.risk: The net move is trivial electrically but does change the schematic, so it is not a build-time fix. Even after the move D1 will probably still be destroyed (it just takes F1 with it, which is the intent), so a builder who reverses the cells replaces two parts instead of an unknown number. If you go to a Schottky, check its 3 V reverse leakage — leakage here is an always-on drain that SW1 cannot switch off. Honest caveat I could not resolve from the files: whether a GBA shell mechanically permits both AA cells to be reversed at all. If it does not, D1 is doing nothing in any case and could be depopulated with zero consequence — it is reverse-biased in normal operation and its 80 V standoff clamps nothing on the positive side. Worth noting that MouseBiteLabs changed this part on the later AGBM-11 (lithium) board to an SMF5.0A-T13 bidirectional TVS, which is a transient suppressor rather than a reverse-polarity clamp — appropriate there because a soldered cell cannot be reversed.
findings.verify_reason: The topology defect and the wrong-description catch are both real and I verified them independently; the fault-clearing timing that justifies the fix is wrong. VERIFIED: ROHM 1SS355VM datasheet (extracted with pypdf) is titled 'Switching Diode (High speed switching)', structure 'Epitaxial planar', package SOD-323FL. Absolute maxima: VR 80 V, VRM 90 V, Io 100 mA, IFM 225 mA, IFSM 500 mA at t=1s, Tj 150C. Characteristics: VF 1.2 V max at IF=100 mA, IR 100 nA max at VR=80 V, Ct 3.0 pF at VR=0.5 V, trr 4.0 ns. Every number the finding quotes is exact, and it is definitively NOT a Schottky — the KiCad Description 'Schottky diode' on D1 and D2 is wrong in the AGBM-01 schematic AND PCB (and in AGBM-02 and AGBM-11 too; I checked all six files). Topology verified by my own netlist dump: D1 pad 1 is the CATHODE (K) on Net-(BT1-+), pad 2 the anode on GND, and Net-(BT1-+) contains only BT1.1, D1.1 and F1.1 — so the reverse-insertion loop is battery -> GND -> D1 -> BT1+ -> battery and does not include F1. That is a genuine design defect and the proposed net move to VBATT is the textbook arrangement. LTC3527 absolute maximum on VIN/VIN1/VIN2 confirmed as -0.3 V to 6 V from the ADI datasheet, so the -3 V excursion is a real abs-max violation. WRONG: 'F1's pre-arc I2t of 0.030 A2s corresponds to ~1.6 ms at 4.4 A'. Same error as the f1-redundant finding — 0.030 A2sec is specified at 50 A and cannot be extrapolated to 4.4 A; the Accu-Guard II table's own 'fusing current within 5 sec = 4.00 A' puts the real clearing time at 4.4 A in the order of seconds. Over that time D1 (IFSM 500 mA for 1 s, ~5 W dissipated) is destroyed many times over, and its failure mode decides the outcome: fail-open and the fuse never clears, fail-short and it clears after seconds of multi-watt dissipation inside a sealed shell. The fix is still worth making — it is the difference between 'the pack can stay shorted forever' and 'the pack is disconnected eventually' — but it should not be sold as a millisecond-scale clear. Also note the 3.3-6.7 A estimate is an upper bound: VF on a 225 mA-rated junction at multiple amps is far above the 1.2 V/100 mA spec, so the actual current is lower. The finding's own honest caveat (can a GBA shell physically accept a reversed AA?) is the load-bearing unknown and remains unresolved.
findings.correction: Keep the net move (D1 cathode from Net-(BT1-+) to VBATT) and keep the 'Description says Schottky, part is a silicon switching diode' correction. Drop the '~1.6 ms' clearing time: at 4.4 A the F0805B2R00 clears in seconds, not milliseconds, per its own 4.00 A/5 s spec, so the realistic outcome is that D1 is destroyed first and the fuse clears only if D1 fails short. If the fix is worth doing at all, pair it with a part that can hold the fault for seconds (the SOD-323 land accepts a 1 A Schottky) — and verify that part's 3 V reverse leakage first, since D1 is permanently across the pack with SW1 off.

findings.title: SW1 carries no load current — the whole battery current bypasses it, so its 70 mohm contact resistance is worth 2 nW. No lever here.
findings.current_part: SW1 = Nidec Copal CSS series compact slide switch. Verified from the Nidec CSS catalogue: contact rating non-switching DC50 V / 100 mA, switching DC12 V / 100 mA, minimum DC20 mV / 1 uA; contact resistance 70 mohm maximum; insulation resistance 100 Mohm min at DC500 V; slider contact, fixed contact and terminal pin are copper alloy, gold-plated; cover SUS304 stainless; 2 mm stroke. Netlist (pinout dump of the fork board): SW1.1 = VBATT, SW1.2 = SW, SW1.3 = SW, SW1.4 = unconnected. The SW net goes ONLY to Q3 emitter, R3 (5.1k), R11 (1k), R12 (100k), R58 (5.1k) and TP20 — a soft-start / enable network. Meanwhile VBATT feeds PTC1 directly, and PTC1.2 = VCC feeds U5 VIN/VIN1/VIN2, L1, L2 and C37. So the converter input is permanently connected to the pack and the switch only gates the LTC3527's SHDN pins via /EN.
findings.proposal: No change. Reporting the answer to the question, because it removes an obvious-looking lever from consideration.
findings.benefit: Zero, and I want to be explicit rather than inflate it. SW current computed from the netlist at V_pack = 3.0 V: R3 5.1k + R4 33k = 38.1k -> 79 uA; R58 5.1k + R63 100k = 105.1k -> 28.5 uA; R11 1k + R24 100k = 101k -> 30 uA; R12 100k -> up to 30 uA when Q1 conducts. Total ~140-170 uA. Dissipation in SW1 at its 70 mohm maximum contact resistance = (170e-6)^2 x 0.070 = 2.0e-9 W = 0.000002 mW. Voltage drop across the contacts = 170 uA x 70 mohm = 12 uV. This is nine orders of magnitude below anything that matters. It is also good design: the stock GBA switches the full battery current through its power switch, whereas AGBM-01 uses the switch only as a logic-level enable, which is why the switch's 100 mA contact rating is not a problem despite the board drawing up to 780 mA. Corollary worth stating: do NOT 'fix' this by routing VBATT through SW1 — that would exceed the switch's 100 mA switching rating by roughly 8x at the overclocked peak. The switch also stays comfortably above its DC20 mV / 1 uA minimum applicable load, and the contacts are gold-plated, so dry-circuit film formation is not a concern.
findings.risk: None. The only downstream consequence of the topology is that the pack is never fully disconnected: with SW1 off, the always-on drain is R9 (100k, VBATT to VFILT) feeding U3's supervisor plus U5's shutdown quiescent current (LTC3827 datasheet gives 0.1 uA typ / 2 uA max in shutdown, not including switch leakage). That is a few microamps at 3 V, i.e. single-digit microwatts — irrelevant against a ~2000 mAh AA pair.
findings.verify_reason: I checked every element and it all holds. Nidec CSS catalogue (extracted with pypdf): STANDARD SPECIFICATIONS give contact rating 'Non-switching: DC50 V, 100 mA / Switching: DC12 V, 100 mA / Minimum: DC20 mV, 1 uA', contact timing non-shorting, contact resistance '70 mOhm maximum', insulation resistance '100 MOhm minimum (DC500 V)', dielectric strength AC500 V 60 s; materials list 'Stainless steel (SUS 304)' and 'Copper alloy, Gold-plated'; ELECTRICAL CHARACTERISTICS give stroke 2 mm. All exactly as stated. My own pad dump: SW1.1 = VBATT, SW1.2 = C = SW, SW1.3 = C = SW, SW1.4 = unconnected. My own net dump of SW: Q3.2 (E), R3.1, R11.1, R12.1, R58.1, SW1.2, SW1.3, TP20 — nothing else, and no load current path. VBATT feeds PTC1 directly. Schematic values confirmed R3 5.1k, R4 33k, R11 1k, R24 100k, R58 5.1k, R63 100k, R12 100k (note the PCB Value for R3/R4 is stale at 1k/10k, but the schematic is authoritative and the finding used the schematic values). Arithmetic redone at 3.0 V: 3.0/38.1k = 78.7 uA; 3.0/105.1k = 28.5 uA; 3.0/101k = 29.7 uA; 3.0/100k = 30 uA; total 137-167 uA. Dissipation (167e-6)^2 x 0.070 = 1.95e-9 W; contact drop 167 uA x 70 mohm = 11.7 uV. Confirmed to be nine orders of magnitude below relevance. The 'do not route VBATT through SW1' corollary is correct — 0.72 A against a 100 mA switching rating is 7x over. LTC3527 shutdown Iq verified from the ADI datasheet electrical table: 0.1 uA typ / 2 uA max, 'Not Including Switch Leakage'; the finding writes 'LTC3827' but that is a typo, the numbers are the LTC3527's. Only cosmetic issue in an otherwise clean finding.
findings.correction: None. Fix the typo 'LTC3827' -> 'LTC3527' in the risk note.

findings.title: SW1's value "CSS-1310B" is not a complete Nidec Copal ordering code — the SMD gull-wing part is CSS-1310TB
findings.current_part: Schematic and PCB Value = "CSS-1310B". The Nidec CSS catalogue's part-number designation is CSS - (poles)(contacts)(setting position)(self-return) (packaging) (terminal shape), where packaging is T = taping or M = magazine and terminal shape is B = gull wing or C = through-hole pins. The catalogue's LIST OF PART NUMBERS for the 3-contact side-setting no-self-return variant contains exactly two entries: CSS-1310TB (gull wing, taping, 1900 pcs/reel) and CSS-1310MC (through-hole pins, magazine, 38 pcs/stick). "CSS-1310B" omits the packaging letter and does not appear in the list.
findings.proposal: CSS-1310TB. The board footprint Bucketmouse:AGB-Switch_CSS-1X10B_Uncentered places SMD rectangular pads on B.Cu, i.e. gull-wing terminals, so the B (gull wing) / T (tape) part is the right one. AGBM-11 uses an even looser value, "CSS-1X10B", so this is a house shorthand rather than a typo, but a builder searching a distributor for "CSS-1310B" gets nothing.
findings.benefit: No electrical effect. Purely a BOM-usability fix.
findings.risk: None. Worth a two-second edit next time the schematic is touched.
findings.verify_reason: Verified against the Nidec CSS catalogue itself, extracted with pypdf. The 'LIST OF PART NUMBERS' table for the 3-contact, side-setting, no-self-return variant contains exactly CSS-1310TB (1,900 pcs/reel) and CSS-1310MC (38 pcs/stick) — precisely the two entries and quantities the finding cites. 'CSS-1310B' is not in that list, so a distributor search on it does fail. I also checked the board: the footprint Bucketmouse:AGB-Switch_CSS-1X10B_Uncentered has five SMD rect pads, all on 'B.Cu'/'B.Mask'/'B.Paste', i.e. gull-wing surface mount — so CSS-1310TB (T = taping, B = gull wing) is the correct orderable code and CSS-1310MC (through-hole, magazine) is not. One caveat worth adding, which the finding overstates: 'CSS-1310B' is not an invented string — it appears in the catalogue's OUTLINE DIMENSIONS section as the drawing label for that switch body ('CSS-1311B / CSS-1310B', and again as '(CSS-1310B)' on the CSS-131xTB dimensional figure). So it is a legitimate Nidec designation for the pole/contact/terminal-shape combination that simply omits the packaging letter, rather than a typo. The practical conclusion — put CSS-1310TB in the BOM — is right either way.
findings.correction: Soften 'does not appear in the list' to 'does not appear in the LIST OF PART NUMBERS'. CSS-1310B does appear in the same catalogue as the outline-drawing designation for the body; it is an incomplete ordering code, not a wrong one.

findings.title: Board copper from BT1 to the LTC3527 is about 6 mohm — 2-5% of the series path. Leave it alone.
findings.current_part: 4-layer board, 35 um (1 oz) copper on F.Cu, In1.Cu, In2.Cu and B.Cu per the stackup block in the .kicad_pcb. Sheet resistance = 1.72e-8 ohm.m / 35e-6 m = 0.491 mohm per square. The battery path is almost entirely pour, not track: Net-(BT1-+) has one F.Cu zone (68.45 mm2 filled, bbox 13.9 x 10.5 mm) plus 7.16 mm of 0.4 mm track; VBATT has an F.Cu zone (11.18 mm2 filled) plus 16.5 mm of 0.5 mm track (that track goes to SW1 and D2, not the load); VCC has an F.Cu zone (11.64 mm2), two B.Cu zones (22.6 mm2 total) plus 3.75 mm of 1.4 mm B.Cu track, two In2.Cu zones (79.37 + 44.56 = 123.9 mm2) and 12 x 0.7/0.3 mm vias. Key positions: BT1 pad 1 (30.54,-16.47) and (31.00,-18.95); F1 pads (32.14,-24.20)/(30.26,-24.20); PTC1 pads (31.90,-28.54)/(31.90,-26.66); U5 VIN pins around (26.15,-41.35)/(28.35,-39.65); L1 pad 1 (28.32,-45.00); L2 pad 1 (28.32,-34.80).
findings.proposal: No change. Documenting the number so the reviewer does not spend a board revision widening copper that is already 20-40x smaller than the parts it feeds.
findings.benefit:
Segment by segment: (a) BT1+ pour to F1 pad 1, ~6 mm through a pour averaging 6.5 mm wide = ~1 square = 0.5 mohm, call it <=1 mohm. (b) VBATT pour, F1 pad 2 to PTC1 pad 1, 4.4 mm span with 11.18 mm2 filled = ~2.5 mm average width = 1.75 squares = 0.9 mohm. (c) VCC: I ran a scanline resistance integral over the In2.Cu VCC fill polygons (script strip.py in the scratchpad), summing dy/w(y) x R_sheet across the full 21.3 mm from y = -24.40 to -45.68: 3.59 mohm to the far end at L1, and about 2.6 mohm to U5's VIN pins. The parallel B.Cu VCC pour and the 1.4 mm B.Cu track reduce that further, so 2-3.5 mohm is the honest range. (d) Vias: a 0.3 mm drill with 25 um plating over the 1.18 mm stack gives an annulus of 0.0255 mm2 and a full-height resistance of ~0.8 mohm; there are 12 on VCC and 3 on VBATT, in parallel groups, so well under 1 mohm total. (e) Ground return is a solid In1.Cu plane plus GND pours on all four layers — sub-milliohm.
Total one-way: ~5-7 mohm. Loss = I^2 R: 0.24 mW at 200 mA, 0.51 at 292 mA, 0.91 at 390 mA, 1.82 at 550 mA, 3.38 at 750 mA. Against F1 + PTC1's 120-240 mohm, the copper is 2-6% of the series path and nothing to fix.
findings.risk: None. The only caveat is that the scanline integral treats the In2 pour as a 1-D conductor with all the current going to the farthest pin, which overestimates it; the real figure is lower, so 6 mohm is a safe upper bound.
findings.verify_reason: I re-derived the geometry from the .kicad_pcb myself and it matches to two decimal places. Stackup block: F.Cu, In1.Cu, In2.Cu, B.Cu all (thickness 0.035), dielectrics 0.1 + 0.84 + 0.1 => 1.18 mm copper-to-copper stack. Sheet resistance 1.72e-8 / 35e-6 = 0.491 mohm/sq, correct. My own polygon-area integration of the filled zones: Net-(BT1-+) F.Cu 68.45 mm2 (bbox x[26.27,39.30] y[-25.10,-14.60]); VBATT F.Cu 11.18 mm2; VCC F.Cu 11.64 mm2, B.Cu 7.76+7.76+7.03 = 22.55 mm2, In2.Cu 79.37 + 44.56 = 123.93 mm2. Every one of those matches the finding exactly. Track lengths: Net-(BT1-+) 7.16 mm of 0.4 mm F.Cu (exact match). Via count by net: 12 vias on VCC and 3 on VBATT, all 0.7 mm pad / 0.3 mm drill — exact match. Via resistance check: annulus for 0.3 mm drill with 25 um plating = pi x (0.175^2 - 0.150^2) = 0.02553 mm2; R = 1.72e-8 x 1.18e-3 / 2.553e-8 = 0.795 mohm. Correct. Independent sanity check on the In2 VCC pour: 79.37 mm2 over a 20.9 mm span gives ~3.8 mm average width = 5.5 squares = 2.7 mohm, consistent with the finding's 2.6-3.6 mohm scanline result. The ~5-7 mohm total and the resulting 0.24 mW at 200 mA / 0.51 at 292 / 3.38 at 750 are right, and the 'leave it alone' conclusion is safe by a wide margin. Two immaterial nits: the finding missed an 86.24 mm2 VBATT pour on B.Cu (x[13.10,29.40] y[-24.40,-11.43]) — but that pour runs to SW1, which carries ~170 uA, so it is off the load path and its omission only makes the estimate more conservative; and the BT1+ zone bbox is 13.03 x 10.50 mm, not 13.9 x 10.5. VBATT track total is 19.4 mm mixed-width, not 16.5 mm of 0.5 mm.
findings.correction: None material. Add the 86.24 mm2 VBATT B.Cu pour to the inventory for completeness (it feeds SW1 only, so it does not change the load-path number).

findings.title: The battery contacts are the one series element with no published spec, and the cells' own 0.3-0.6 ohm ESR dwarfs everything on the board
findings.current_part: BT1 = Bucketmouse:AGB-Battery, four through-hole pads (two per polarity, 2 x 3.5 mm oval and 2 x 2 mm custom, 1.2 mm drills, on all copper layers). The schematic Source field points at retrogamerepairshop's GBA replacement battery contact terminals. I could find NO published contact-resistance figure for that part or for OEM GBA terminals — the vendor page and the aftermarket listings describe them only qualitatively ('specs very close to OEM', 'reduce electrical resistance'). Treat any number for these contacts as UNVERIFIED.
findings.proposal: Two actions, both free. (1) Measure rather than guess: with the console running at a known current, measure the DC drop from the AA cell's own terminal to the BT1 pad on the PCB, and divide. That converts the unknown into a number in about a minute and tells you whether it belongs in this domain's budget at all. (2) If the contacts are visibly oxidised or corroded — which is the normal state of a 20-year-old GBA — clean or replace them, because that is a zero-cost change with a potentially larger effect than every component swap in this review combined.
findings.benefit: Cannot be quantified from published data, and I am not going to invent a number. What I CAN anchor is the surrounding context: the Energizer E91 datasheet gives nominal internal resistance of 150-300 mohm per fresh AA alkaline, so the pack contributes 300-600 mohm of series resistance — 2 to 5 times the entire board-side path (120-240 mohm as built, 65-115 mohm after the recommended swaps). At the 750 mA overclocked peak the cells alone drop 225-450 mV and dissipate 169-338 mW internally, versus 90-180 mV and 68-135 mW on the board. That is the honest framing for this whole domain: the board-side loss is real and worth attacking, but the pack's own ESR is the dominant term and cannot be touched. It also means contact resistance would have to be in the tens of milliohms per interface before it rivals the cells; on a clean pair of contacts it will not be, and on a corroded pair it may exceed everything else on this list. Note this also means the input path is where a switch to NiMH cells would change the picture, since NiMH ESR is far lower — but I have not verified a NiMH ESR figure so I will not put a number on it.
findings.risk: None. The risk is analytical: if you do not measure the contacts, you may spend a board revision on 20 mohm of PPTC while a corroded terminal is contributing more.
findings.verify_reason: The one hard number is verified and the honesty about the unverified one is exactly right. Energizer E91 product datasheet, extracted with pypdf, states verbatim: 'Nominal IR: 150 to 300 milliohms (fresh)', nominal voltage 1.5 V, ANSI-15A / IEC-LR6. Two cells in series therefore give 300-600 mohm, as claimed. Arithmetic redone: at 750 mA the pack drops 0.750 x (0.30..0.60) = 225-450 mV and dissipates 0.5625 x (0.30..0.60) = 169-338 mW internally; the board side at the corrected 0.120-0.230 ohm drops 90-173 mV and dissipates 68-129 mW. The framing — pack ESR is 2 to 5 times the whole board-side path and is untouchable — is correct and is the most useful sentence in this domain. BT1 footprint confirmed as four through-hole pads on all copper layers with 1.2 mm drills. I could find no published contact-resistance figure for the retrogamerepairshop terminals either, and the finding's refusal to invent one is the right call. Worth adding, from the numbers above: at 750 mA the pack sags to roughly 1.95-2.17 V from a 2.4 V starting point, which is at or below the TPS3840DL20's 2.0 V cutoff — so the 750 mA column in every finding in this domain is a bounding case, not an operating point.
findings.correction: Board-side path is 0.120-0.230 ohm (90-173 mV, 68-129 mW at 750 mA), using the corrected 0.150 R1max. Add the observation that 750 mA is not a sustainable operating point: the pack sag it implies puts VFILT at or under the supervisor's 2.0 V cutoff.

findings.title: Evaluated and rejected: an ideal-diode / eFuse in place of F1+PTC1 is verifiably WORSE at 1.8 V pack voltage
findings.current_part: F1 + PTC1 in series, 0.120-0.240 ohm as built, 0.065-0.115 ohm after the recommended swaps. The attraction of an eFuse or ideal diode is that it would collapse overcurrent protection, reverse-battery protection and the series drop into one part.
findings.proposal: Rejected, with numbers. The obvious candidate is the TI LM66100 (5.5 V, 1.5 A ideal diode with input polarity protection, SC-70-6/DCK), whose recommended input range starts at 1.5 V, low enough for a 2 x AA pack. But its on-resistance is specified against VIN, and it degrades badly at the bottom of the pack: R_ON at IOUT = -200 mA is 79 mohm typ / 95 mohm max at VIN = 5 V; 91 typ / 110 max at 3.6 V; and 141 mohm typ / 180 mohm max at 25 C at VIN = 1.8 V, rising to 210 mohm over -40 to 85 C. At the operating point that matters most — low battery, high current — a single LM66100 is worse than the two parts it would replace and roughly 3x the upgraded pair. Its quiescent current is excellent (0.15 uA typ, 0.3 uA max) but that is not the constraint here. The other family, integrated eFuses with current limiting (TPS259x class), generally do not operate below ~2.7 V, so they are simply out of range for a pack that reaches 1.8 V. A discrete series FET (P-channel on the high side or N-channel in the ground return) faces the same physics — you need R_ds(on) specified at V_GS = 1.8 V, and I could not verify a SOT-23 part whose datasheet specifies R_ds(on) at that gate drive below the 15-65 mohm of the upgraded PPTC, so I will not name one. It would also add no overcurrent protection and would lift the board ground off the battery negative, which complicates the audio-jack reference.
findings.benefit: Negative. Replacing 0.065-0.115 ohm with 141-210 mohm would COST, not save: at 390 mA the delta of roughly +0.07 to +0.13 ohm is 11-20 mW, and at 750 mA it is 39-73 mW.
findings.risk: The value of this finding is that it closes off a plausible-sounding direction with a verified datasheet number rather than an opinion. If the design ever moved to a lithium cell (AGBM-11 territory, 3.0-4.2 V) the LM66100's 91 mohm at 3.6 V becomes competitive and the conclusion would flip — so this rejection is specific to the 2 x AA voltage range.
findings.verify_reason: The rejection is correct and rests on numbers I verified line by line. TI LM66100 datasheet, extracted with pypdf: 'Wide operating voltage range: 1.5 V - 5.5 V', 'Maximum continuous current (IMAX): 1.5 A', and the RON table reads 'RON ON-State Resistance IOUT = -200 mA VIN = 5 V, 25C 79 typ 95 max; -40 to 85C 110; -40 to 125C 120' / 'VIN = 3.6 V, 25C 91 typ 110 max; -40 to 85C 125; -40 to 125C 140' / 'VIN = 1.8 V, 25C 141 typ 180 max; -40 to 85C 210; -40 to 125C 230' — every figure the finding cites is exact, including the 210 mohm over-temperature number that does the work. Quiescent current 150 nA typ at 3.6 V confirmed. So a single LM66100 at the bottom of a 2xAA pack is 141-210 mohm against 65-115 mohm for the upgraded pair, and the conclusion that it costs rather than saves is sound. Its arithmetic is loose but in the safe direction: the like-for-like delta is +0.076 ohm (best vs best) to +0.095 ohm (worst vs worst), not '+0.07 to +0.13', so the cost is 11.6-14.5 mW at 390 mA and 42.8-53.4 mW at 750 mA rather than the wider 11-20 / 39-73 quoted. One conceptual slip worth flagging: the LM66100 is an ideal diode with reverse-current blocking, not an eFuse — it has no overcurrent limit at all, so it would not 'collapse overcurrent protection, reverse-battery protection and the series drop into one part'; it would delete overcurrent protection entirely on top of costing resistance. That makes the rejection stronger, not weaker. I did not independently verify the TPS259x minimum operating voltage or the claim that no SOT-23 FET specifies Rds(on) at Vgs = 1.8 V below 65 mohm; treat those two sentences as unverified. Value of the finding is real: it closes a plausible direction with a datasheet number.
findings.correction: Delta is +0.076 to +0.095 ohm, i.e. a cost of 11.6-14.5 mW at 390 mA and 42.8-53.4 mW at 750 mA (the quoted 11-20 / 39-73 mW ranges are wider than the numbers support). Also: the LM66100 is an ideal diode, not an eFuse — it provides no current limit, so it cannot replace F1/PTC1 functionally either. The TPS259x <2.7 V claim and the SOT-23 FET claim are unverified.

findings.title: F1 and PTC1 pads use thermal relief to their pours — worth ~0.5 mohm, but solid connections would also raise the PPTC's effective hold current
findings.current_part: Both F1 pads and both PTC1 pads carry (zone_connect 1) with (thermal_bridge_width 0.5), i.e. KiCad thermal relief with 0.5 mm spokes, against the F.Cu BT1+, VBATT and VCC pours. Pads are 0.975 x 1.4 mm roundrect. Zone thermal gap is the KiCad default.
findings.proposal: Set zone_connect 2 (solid fill) on all four pads. PCB file edit only, no land pattern change, no schematic change.
findings.benefit: Small and I will not inflate it. Four spokes of 0.5 mm across a ~0.5 mm gap is 2 mm of effective width over 0.5 mm = 0.25 square = 0.12 mohm per pad; if only two spokes form, 0.25 mohm. Across four pads that is 0.5-1.0 mohm, worth 0.04-0.09 mW at 292 mA and 0.28-0.56 mW at 750 mA. Rounding error on its own. The reason to do it anyway is thermal, not electrical: a PPTC's hold current is set entirely by how fast it sheds heat, and Littelfuse specify I_hold in 20 C still air with no board heatsinking assumed. Bonding both PTC1 pads solidly to the VBATT and VCC pours (11-12 mm2 of F.Cu each, plus the 124 mm2 In2.Cu VCC plane through the vias) gives the device a real heatsink and pushes its effective hold current up, which is exactly the margin the ClockxControl is eating into. Same argument in reverse for F1: solid pads make the fuse slightly slower to open, which is a mild negative, so if you only change one, change PTC1.
findings.risk: Solid pads on 0805 parts are marginally harder to hand-solder and slightly more prone to tombstoning in reflow because the two ends heat unevenly — though with a large pour on both ends that asymmetry is small here. For F1 specifically, better heatsinking raises its effective rating, i.e. slows the fuse; that is a small protection regression, so restricting the change to PTC1 is the conservative option. I have no measured data on how much the effective hold current actually rises, so treat that part as directional, not quantified.
findings.verify_reason: The observation is real but the already-tiny benefit is overstated by 2x, because the thermal gap is half what the finding assumed. I dumped the pads directly: F1 pad 1 and 2, and PTC1 pad 1 and 2, all carry (zone_connect 1) with (thermal_bridge_width 0.5), pad size 0.975 x 1.4 roundrect — confirmed. But the finding says 'Zone thermal gap is the KiCad default' and then computes with a 0.5 mm gap. The VCC/VBATT/BT1+ zone fill blocks explicitly set (thermal_gap 0.25) (thermal_bridge_width 0.25). The pad-level 0.5 mm overrides the spoke width, but the gap the spokes must bridge is 0.25 mm, not 0.5 mm. Redoing it: 4 spokes x 0.5 mm = 2.0 mm effective width across a 0.25 mm gap = 0.125 square = 0.491 x 0.125 = 0.061 mohm per pad (0.123 mohm if only two spokes form), i.e. 0.25-0.5 mohm across four pads, not 0.5-1.0. Loss recovered: 0.021-0.043 mW at 292 mA and 0.14-0.28 mW at 750 mA. That is half of the already-negligible claim. The electrical case is therefore even weaker than presented; the finding is honest that it is rounding error. The thermal argument (solid pads heatsink the PPTC and raise its effective hold current) is directionally sound — Littelfuse specify Ihold in 20C still air with no board heatsinking assumed — but Littelfuse publish no board-thermal derating for the Low Rho series, so the magnitude is unquantifiable, exactly as the finding admits. The reverse argument for F1 (solid pads slow the fuse) is correct and is the reason to restrict any change to PTC1. Keep the finding, halve the number, and treat it as a free rider on a PCB revision rather than a reason for one.
findings.correction: Zone thermal_gap is explicitly 0.25 mm in the VCC/VBATT/BT1+ fills, not the assumed 0.5 mm. Spoke resistance is 0.061 mohm per pad (0.123 if only two spokes form), so the total is 0.25-0.5 mohm, worth 0.02-0.04 mW at 292 mA and 0.14-0.28 mW at 750 mA — half the claimed figure.

findings.title: None of the AGBM-01 vs AGBM-02 29 mW idle gap comes from this domain — the protection parts are identical on both boards
findings.current_part: AGBM-01 rev 1.2 schematic: F1 = F0805B2R00FSTR, PTC1 = 0805L075SLYR, D1 = D2 = 1SS355VMTE-17, SW1 = CSS-1310B. I pulled the same fields from MouseBiteLabs' AGBM-02 schematic and PCB and they are character-for-character identical (AGBM-02's PCB even carries the correct Values where AGBM-01's carries the stale 0467001.NR strings).
findings.proposal: No change. Recording it so this domain is correctly excluded from the hunt for the 29 mW idle delta.
findings.benefit: Zero saving; a scoping result. AGBM-01 idles at 170 mW and AGBM-02 at 141 mW. At the self-consistent idle current (170 mW / 2.4 V = 71 mA) the entire F1 + PTC1 series path dissipates 0.60-1.20 mW, i.e. 0.35-0.71% of the idle figure — and since both boards carry the same parts, the contribution to the DELTA is exactly zero. The 29 mW must come from the converter (LTC3527 with 2 x 4.7 uH inductors vs 2 x TPS63802 with 0.47 uH), not from the input path. Corollary for the reviewer's framing: the brief asks for the I2R loss as a percentage of the 170 mW idle, but the 200/350/550 mA currents in the brief do not correspond to the idle condition. Reported both ways: at 200 mA the loss is 4.8-9.6 mW (2.8-5.6% of 170 mW, 0.69-1.37% of 700 mW); at 350 mA it is 14.7-29.4 mW (8.6-17.3% / 2.1-4.2%); at 550 mA it is 36.3-72.6 mW (21.4-42.7% / 5.2-10.4%). The physically meaningful pair is the self-consistent one: 0.6-1.2 mW at idle (0.35-0.71%) and 10.2-20.5 mW at 700 mW in-use (1.5-2.9%).
findings.risk: None.
findings.verify_reason: I reproduced the cross-design comparison independently with my own s-expression parser over all six files. AGBM-02 schematic: F1 = F0805B2R00FSTR, PTC1 = 0805L075SLYR, D1 = D2 = 1SS355VMTE-17, SW1 = CSS-1310B — character-for-character identical to AGBM-01's schematic. AGBM-02's PCB carries the same correct values where AGBM-01's PCB carries the stale 0467001.NR strings. So the protection/input path is genuinely identical between the two boards and its contribution to the 29 mW idle delta is exactly zero. The scoping conclusion — the delta must live in the converter (one LTC3527 with 2 x 4.7 uH vs two TPS63802 with 0.47 uH) — is correct and is a useful negative result. Arithmetic redone with the corrected 0.230 ohm upper bound: at 170 mW / 2.4 V = 70.8 mA the F1+PTC1 loss is 0.005 x (0.120..0.230) = 0.60-1.15 mW, i.e. 0.35-0.68% of idle. At 200 mA: 4.8-9.2 mW. At 350 mA: 14.7-28.2 mW. At 550 mA: 36.3-69.6 mW. At 292 mA (700 mW at 2.4 V): 10.2-19.6 mW, 1.5-2.8% of 700 mW. All within a percent of the finding's figures, the small differences being the 0.240 -> 0.230 correction. The point that the brief's 200/350/550 mA currents do not correspond to the idle condition, and that quoting the loss as a percentage of 170 mW at 550 mA is physically meaningless, is well made and correct.

findings.title: CP1/CP2/CP3 are polarized tantalums on a symmetric MLCC land pattern with no polarity marking anywhere on the board
findings.current_part: Schematic symbol is "Polarized capacitor, small symbol"; the Source field resolves to Kyocera AVX TPSB107K010R0400 - 100 uF, 10 V, case B (EIA 1210 tantalum = 3528-21 metric, 3.50 x 2.80 x 1.90 mm, terminal width W1 2.20 mm, terminal length A 0.80 mm, S min 1.40 mm), ESR max 400 mOhm at 100 kHz, 0.461 A rms at 25 C, DCL max 10 uA (Kyocera AVX TPS series ratings table, 10 V @ 85 C block). The PCB footprint is Bucketmouse:C_1210_3225Metric_Boxed_2: roundrect pads 1.15 x 2.70 mm at +/-1.475 mm, and the F.SilkS artwork is two identical brackets at x = -2.3 and x = +2.3 with no stripe, no chamfer and no "+". I dumped the footprint's six F.SilkS fp_line entries directly from the .kicad_pcb and they are mirror-symmetric.
findings.proposal: Three separable fixes, cheapest first. (a) Add a polarity mark: an F.SilkS stripe or a "+" beside pad 1 of each of CP1/CP2/CP3, plus a pin-1 chamfer on the F.Fab body. Zero cost, zero electrical change. (b) Note that the land is dimensionally fine for the case-B tantalum even though it is named 3225: pads run from 0.825 to 2.075 mm from centre, the tantalum's terminals from 0.95 to 1.75 mm, so there is 0.125 mm inner and 0.325 mm outer overhang and the 2.70 mm pad comfortably covers the 2.20 mm terminal. The only geometric error is the courtyard, which is drawn for a 3.2 x 2.5 mm body and is 0.3 mm undersize in both axes for the 3.5 x 2.8 mm tantalum; the nearest neighbour is 1.0 mm away (CP1/CP2/CP3 are on a 3.8 mm pitch) so nothing collides today. (c) If you would rather not rely on silk, use a non-polar 100 uF 1210 MLCC, which is what the footprint is actually named for - but read the cp1-reverse-bias finding first, because that decision interacts with it.
findings.benefit: No power saving; this is a build-defect guard. Consequence if it is got wrong: CP2 and CP3 sit with a permanent 1.25 V DC forward bias (LM4853 SE outputs are biased at VAUD/2 = 2.5/2 = 1.25 V, with R19/R20 1k to AGND on the load side). Fitted backwards they see 1.25 V continuous reverse, which is 12.5 % of the 10 V rating - above Kyocera AVX's own published limit of "10 % of rated voltage to a maximum of 1 volt at 25 C", and that limit is explicitly stated to apply only to short excursions and "should never be used to determine the maximum reverse voltage under which a capacitor can be used permanently". The failure mode for a reversed MnO2 tantalum is a dead short across a 100 mA-class audio output. On a hobbyist hand-built board with three identical unmarked 1210 pads, this is a when-not-if.
findings.risk: The silk fix has no risk. The courtyard fix is cosmetic unless someone later moves parts near CP1-CP3. Adding a polarity stripe requires a new fab run, so for boards already made the mitigation is documentation only.
findings.verify_reason: Core claim CONFIRMED, two geometric numbers wrong. Verified myself: CP1/CP2/CP3 use lib_id Device:C_Polarized_Small (Audio.kicad_sch line ~9497) with Source https://www.digikey.com/short/332b01qh, which I resolved to Kyocera AVX TPSB107K010R0400 - 100 uF, 10 V, molded tantalum, ESR 400 mOhm @100kHz, case 1411(3528 Metric)/1210, Active. From the TPS datasheet ratings table I confirmed the exact row TPSB107*010#0400: 100 uF, 10 V, DCL max 10 uA, DF 8%, ESR max 400 mOhm, 0.461 A rms @25C - every number in the finding is right. Case B dims confirmed verbatim from the same PDF: L 3.50, W 2.80, H 1.90, W1 2.20, A 0.80 (+0.30/-0.20), S min 1.40 mm, EIA 1210 / metric 3528-21. I dumped the footprint from the fork .kicad_pcb: pads roundrect 1.15 x 2.70 at +/-1.475, six F.SilkS fp_lines forming mirror-symmetric brackets at x = -2.3 and +2.3, no stripe, no chamfer, no '+' - polarity claim CONFIRMED. CP1 at (106.2,-23.1), CP2 (106.2,-26.9, rot 180), CP3 (106.2,-19.3): 3.8 mm pitch, 1.0 mm body-to-body, confirmed. Reverse-voltage quotes confirmed VERBATIM from revtant.pdf: '10% of rated voltage to a maximum of 1 volt at 25 degC' and 'These guidelines apply for short excursions and should never be used to determine the maximum reverse voltage under which a capacitor can be used permanently.' CP2/CP3 polarity confirmed from the netlist (pad 1 = anode = LM4853 SE output at VAUD/2, pad 2 = jack + R19/R20 1k to AGND), so a reversed part does sit at 1.25 V continuous reverse. CORRECTIONS: (1) pad copper runs 0.900 to 2.050 mm from centre (1.475 - 0.575 and 1.475 + 0.575), NOT 0.825 to 2.075; against the tantalum terminals at 0.95-1.75 mm that is 0.05 mm inner and 0.30 mm outer overhang, not 0.125/0.325. The conclusion (land is dimensionally fine, 2.70 mm pad covers the 2.20 mm W1) survives. (2) The courtyard is NOT undersize. It is +/-2.30 x +/-1.60 = 4.60 x 3.20 mm, which is LARGER than the 3.50 x 2.80 mm tantalum by 0.55 mm/side in x and 0.20 mm/side in y. The 0.3 mm shortfall the finding computed is in the F.Fab body outline (3.2 x 2.5 mm), not the courtyard. So the only geometric defect is a cosmetic F.Fab rectangle, and the 'nothing collides today' reassurance was never needed. (3) Mitigation the finding omits: a case-B TPS part carries a printed polarity band on the anode end, so this is a build-aid gap, not an unmarked part.

findings.title: CP1 is a polarized tantalum carrying bidirectional AC with zero DC bias - the speaker BTL output reverse-biases it past AVX's own 1 V limit
findings.current_part: CP1 = TPSB107K010R0400, 100 uF 10 V case-B MnO2 tantalum, ESR max 400 mOhm at 100 kHz. Topology from the netlist: U6 (LM4853) pin BTL+ -> CP1.1 -> CP1.2 = SP1.2; SP1.1 -> U6 LOUT/BTL-. So CP1 sits in series with the 8 Ohm AGB speaker inside the bridge. The LM4853 datasheet states plainly that "Since the differential outputs, BTL OUT- and BTL OUT+, are biased at half-supply, no net DC voltage exists across the load. This eliminates the need for the output coupling capacitor that a single supply, single-ended amplifier configuration requires." So CP1 has 0 V DC across it by design, and the whole signal swing appears across it as bidirectional AC. Speaker impedance 8 Ohm (replacement-part specs for the 23 mm AGB/GBC speaker, distributor data, not a Nintendo datasheet - treat as verified-by-distributor).
findings.proposal: Replace CP1 (only) with a non-polar 100 uF 1210 X5R/X7R MLCC of >= 10 V rating on the identical land - the footprint is literally named C_1210_3225Metric, so this is the part the pads were drawn for and it is a drop-in with no board change. Leave CP2/CP3 as tantalums: they have a proper 1.25 V forward DC bias and are correctly applied. If you prefer to keep a tantalum at CP1, the alternative is to accept the exposure and document it; raising the voltage rating does NOT help, because AVX's guideline caps reverse voltage at 1 V absolute regardless of rating.
findings.benefit: Reliability, plus about 1-2.5 mW of recovered audio power at loud volume. Reverse-voltage arithmetic: |Zc| of 100 uF is 31.8 Ohm at 50 Hz, 15.9 Ohm at 100 Hz, 8.0 Ohm at 200 Hz, 4.0 Ohm at 400 Hz. The fraction of the amplifier's output that appears across CP1 is |Zc|/|8 + Zc| = 0.97, 0.89, 0.71 and 0.45 respectively. The LM4853 on a 2.5 V rail can swing roughly 1.5 Vrms differential before clipping, so a loud 100 Hz passage puts ~1.3 Vrms = 1.9 Vpk across CP1, and the negative half-cycle reverse-biases it to ~1.9 V - about twice AVX's "10 % of rated to a maximum of 1 volt at 25 C" figure. Even a modest 1.0 Vrms at 200 Hz reaches 0.71 Vrms = 1.0 Vpk, exactly at the limit. Power side: at 50 mW into the speaker, Irms = sqrt(0.05/8) = 79 mA, so CP1's 400 mOhm ESR burns 0.079^2 x 0.4 = 2.5 mW; a 100 uF MLCC at roughly 5 mOhm recovers essentially all of that, and also raises delivered power by 20*log10(8.4/8.25) = 0.16 dB. At 20 mW output the recovery is 1.0 mW.
findings.risk: Two real downsides to the MLCC. (1) Class-II ceramic has an AC voltage coefficient, so a 1-2 V swing across it modulates its own capacitance and produces low-order distortion in exactly the band where the cap is doing work (below ~400 Hz). (2) MLCCs are piezoelectric and a 3225 part carrying 80 mA of audio current can sing audibly. Against that, the high-pass corner with 8 Ohm + 0.4 Ohm ESR is 189 Hz (1/(2*pi*8.4*100e-6)), and TI's own note is that portable speakers "have little ability to reproduce signals below 150 Hz" - so the frequency region where the ceramic misbehaves is the region the speaker cannot reproduce anyway. The counter-risk of doing nothing is a slow-degrading tantalum in a hand-built console. Confidence is not higher because AVX's reverse-voltage guideline is explicitly written for DC excursions, and audio half-cycles are the mildest kind of excursion; the practical failure rate on existing AGBM builds is unknown to me.
findings.verify_reason: Reliability half stands; power claim and drop-in claim both fail. CONFIRMED from the board file: CP1.1 = Net-(U6-BTL+), CP1.2 = Net-(CP1-Pad2) = SP1.2, SP1.1 = Net-(U6-LOUT/BTL-). CP1 is in series with the speaker inside the bridge. The TI quote is VERBATIM correct (LM4853 SNAS155E, Operation section): 'Since the differential outputs, BTL OUT- and BTL OUT+, are biased at half-supply, no net DC voltage exists across the load.' I also found the number the finding missed: VOS BTL OUT+ to OUT- is 5 mV typ / 40 mV max, so DC across CP1 is <=40 mV - effectively zero, confirming the misapplication. Impedance fractions all reproduce: 31.83/32.82 = 0.970, 15.92/17.82 = 0.893, 7.958/11.28 = 0.705, 3.979/8.935 = 0.445. One datasheet correction in the finding's favour: LM4853 Operating Ratings are 2.4 V <= VDD <= 5.5 V, so VAUD = 2.5 V is in spec (a WebFetch summariser told me 2.7 V; the actual table says 2.4 V). POWER CLAIM REFUTED IN MAGNITUDE. 50 mW into the 8 Ohm speaker is unreachable inside the measured envelope. MouseBiteLabs' 'roughly 75% efficient supply ... specifically for the audio' is U4, the NCV8164 2.5 V LDO off VOUT3: 2.5/3.336 = 0.749, exactly 75%. So the 50-100 mW audio figure leaves the amplifier at most ~75 mW, and less after ~4.5 mW of LM4853 quiescent (1.8 mA at 2.5 V, datasheet) plus TLV9364 and the VAUD 100k dividers. Class-AB BTL from 2.5 V: P_supply = VDD x 2 x Ipk/pi. At 75 mW, Ipk = 75e-3 x pi/(2 x 2.5) = 47 mA, Po = Ipk^2 x R/2 = 8.8 mW, Irms = 33 mA, CP1 ESR loss = 0.033^2 x 0.4 = 0.44 mW. At a more realistic 60 mW to the output stage it is 0.29 mW. So the recovery is 0.3-0.45 mW at full volume, not 1-2.5 mW - overstated 2-6x - and it exists only while loud audio is playing. Against 792-1175 mW in use that is 0.04%. REVERSE EXPOSURE ALSO OVERSTATED: at Ipk = 47 mA the peak across CP1 is 0.047 x 15.92 = 0.75 Vpk at 100 Hz, UNDER the 1 V guideline; it only passes 1 V for near-clipping content below ~80 Hz, which the finding's own argument says the speaker cannot reproduce. So this is a transient-peak exposure, not the routine one implied. DROP-IN CLAIM REFUTED AS STATED: the land is fine, but the only 100 uF 10 V X5R 1210 I could find (Murata GRM32ER61A107ME20K) has a 2.70 mm max seated height against 1.90+0.20 mm for case B - 0.6-0.8 mm taller on F.Cu next to the jack, in a shell the context calls 'extremely tight' - and DigiKey shows it out of stock with a Nov-2026 factory date. Height clearance is unverified, so this is not a no-risk drop-in. Finally, the '0.16 dB' delivered-power figure is wrong: 0.4 Ohm to ~0 Ohm in series with 8 Ohm is 20log10(8.4/8.0) = 0.42 dB.

findings.title: The SRAM has no decoupling capacitor within 7 mm of any VDD2 pin, and ECO-5 made it worse
findings.current_part: VDD2 pads on U2 and their nearest VDD2 capacitor, computed from the fork board file: pin 12 (81.31, -58.05) -> C46 (1 uF) at 9.9 mm; pin 16 (81.31, -56.05) -> C46 at 8.0 mm; pin 37, stock outer column (95.10, -58.05) -> C8 (0.1 uF) at 9.9 mm; pin 37, CY62157 third column (100.31, -58.05) -> C8 at 7.1 mm. For comparison the CPU is properly served: U1 pin 44 has C15 at 2.6 mm and C46 at 4.5 mm, pin 65 has C16 at 2.4 mm and C48 at 3.6 mm, pins 115/117 have C45/C47 at 2.5-2.7 mm and C52/C53 at 3.1-3.7 mm. ECO-5 moved C8 from (100.8, -59.3) - 5.7 mm from the stock pin 37 - to (103.0, -64.9), which is 7.1 mm from the pad a CY62157 actually lands on. The fork's own README also records that "Five GND stitching vias and eleven plane segments under the new body were removed (re-stitch before fab)", so the return path under U2 is currently degraded as well.
findings.proposal: Add two 0603 caps on B.Cu directly under the SRAM, where the layer is empty: one 0.1 uF (C0603C104K5RACTU, same as C8) at roughly (82.0, -56.0) to serve pins 12/16, and one 0.1 uF at roughly (94.0, -55.5) to serve pin 37. Both locations are clear of every existing B.Cu footprint in that region (nearest are RA1 ending at y = -58.5, R35 at -58.5, R65 and C72 at -57.3, U14 at -56.5) and both sit outside the B.Cu cartridge rule area, which forbids pads only for y between -54.2 and -32.2. Optionally move C8 back toward pin 37 as well. Route each cap's GND pad to In1.Cu with its own via next to the pad, not through a shared stub. Then finish the ECO-5 re-stitching the README already calls for.
findings.benefit: No power saving - this is a signal-integrity fix. The size of the problem: at 8-10 mm the loop from an SRAM VCC pin to the nearest cap is roughly 16-20 mm of go-and-return path. Using the usual ~1 nH/mm rule of thumb for a trace over a nearby plane (this is an engineering estimate, not a datasheet number) that is 15-20 nH, whose impedance at 100 MHz is 9-13 Ohm. Bringing a cap to 2 mm cuts that by roughly a factor of four. What saves the current board from this being a fault rather than a weakness is that VDD2 is a plane, not a trace: the In2.Cu VDD2 zone spans x 16.8-101.8, y -63.2 to -31.6 and therefore covers every U2 VDD2 pad, sitting over a solid In1.Cu ground plane. That plane pair is what is actually doing the high-frequency work today. With the ClockxControl at 1.75x the SRAM is cycled at 7.34 MHz instead of 4.19 MHz, so edge-rate current demand rises by the same factor and the margin this design has been getting away with shrinks proportionally.
findings.risk: Low. Two 0603 caps and two vias. The only real risk is putting them where they foul the CY62157 body or the re-poured planes, so they must be placed and DRC'd in KiCad rather than trusted from my coordinates - I checked footprint bounding boxes and the B.Cu rule area, not the finished copper. Note also that if you populate an original salvaged GBA RAM instead of the CY62157, pin 37 sits at x = 95.10 and the second cap should move accordingly (or be placed midway to serve both).
findings.verify_reason: I recomputed every distance from the fork board file independently and they match to 0.01 mm. U2 VDD2 pads: pin 12 (81.31,-58.05), pin 16 (81.31,-56.05), pin 37 (100.31,-58.05, the CY62157 third column). Nearest VDD2 capacitor pads: pin 12 -> C46.1 (78.70,-48.475) = 9.92 mm (finding 9.9); pin 16 -> C46.1 = 8.01 mm (8.0); pin 37 -> C8.1 (102.225,-64.90) = 7.11 mm (7.1). CPU comparison also exact: U1.44 -> C15 2.62 / C46 4.51; U1.65 -> C16 2.39 / C48 3.58; U1.115 -> C47 2.59 / C45 2.67 / C52 3.75; U1.117 -> C45 2.47 / C47 3.04 / C52 3.06. ECO-5 regression CONFIRMED from the stock board: agbm01/AGBM-01_AA_1-2.kicad_pcb has C8 at (100.8,-59.3) and U2 pin 37 at (95.10,-58.05) = 5.7 mm; the fork moved C8 to (103.0,-64.9), which is 7.11 mm from the CY62157 pin 37 and 9.88 mm from a salvaged-RAM pin 37. Worse in both cases. README quote is VERBATIM: 'Five GND stitching vias and eleven plane segments under the new body were removed (re-stitch before fab - see below).' Placement legality checked: the B.Cu rule area really is x 33.1-105.1, y -54.2 to -32.2 with '(pads not_allowed) (footprints not_allowed)', so both proposed spots (y = -56.0 and -55.5) sit outside it. Nearest B.Cu footprint centres are C19 at 4.74 mm / RA1 at 4.94 mm from (82.0,-56.0), and C72 at 3.31 mm / R65 3.97 / U14 4.69 from (94.0,-55.5) - all comfortably clear for 0603s. The 1 nH/mm figure is correctly flagged as an estimate, and the finding correctly limits its own severity by noting the In2.Cu VDD2 zone over the In1.Cu ground plane is what carries the HF work today. Two small nits, neither fatal: 'no cap within 7 mm' is true only just (7.11 mm), and the finding does not note that a B.Cu cap under an F.Cu SRAM reaches the pin through via + In2 plane, which is a good path but not the 2 mm equivalent it is compared against. This is the strongest finding in the set.

findings.title: The ClockxControl taps VDD3 at cartridge pad S1, 43.5 mm from the nearest bypass capacitor and 68 mm from its load switch
findings.current_part: Verified from the fork netlist: P1 pad S1 = net VDD3, at (96.90, -35.20) on F.Cu. Nearest VDD3 capacitor is C69 (1 uF) at 43.5 mm; then C49 (1 uF) at 44.6 mm and C5 (0.1 uF) at 44.8 mm. The rail's source, U18 (TPS22917 load switch), is at (29.47, -27.30) on B.Cu - 68 mm away. Total VDD3 decoupling on the whole board after derating is 3 x 1 uF at 0.875 uF each plus 4 x 0.1 uF at 0.100 uF each = 3.03 uF, and none of it is anywhere near the tap. VDD3 does have an In2.Cu plane pour (x 23.6-98.1, y -52.2 to -26.6) which reaches S1 with about 1.2 mm to spare in x.
findings.proposal: Add a 1 uF 16 V X7R 0603 (KEMET C0603C105K4RACTU - already on the BOM as C45-C51 etc., so no new line item) and a 0.1 uF 50 V X7R 0603 (C0603C104K5RACTU, also already on the BOM) on F.Cu at roughly (100.5, -37.0), about 4 mm from S1. That location is clear of P1's courtyard (which ends at x = 97.65), clear of R37 (98.37 to 99.83 in x, -34.48 to -31.52 in y) and - importantly - outside the ECO-6 ClockxControl mezzanine window, which occupies x 82.625-101.275, y -50.950 to -38.950 on F.Cu. B.Cu is not available there: the cartridge rule area forbids pads for x 33.1-105.1, y -54.2 to -32.2.
findings.benefit: No measurable power saving; the argument is clock jitter, not droop. The module contains the oscillator that drives the CPU's XIN, so ripple and noise on its 3.3 V supply translate directly into period jitter on a 7.34 MHz clock feeding a salvaged CPU that was specified for 4.194 MHz - the one part of this build with the least characterisation margin. Droop is genuinely not the concern: the module's ~12 mA over a plane pair spanning 43 mm is maybe a few nH of spreading inductance, and 12 mA through that is nothing. The concern is that there is currently zero local charge reservoir for whatever the module's internal switching does, and the fix costs two 0603s of parts already on the BOM.
findings.risk: Very low electrically. The practical risk is mechanical: the area around P1's S1 pad is congested and the ClockxControl mezzanine window is immediately below it, so the placement must be confirmed in KiCad against the mezzanine keepout and the cart-slot shell. My coordinates come from footprint bounding boxes, not from routed copper.
findings.verify_reason: Every measurement is exactly right; the defect itself is never demonstrated. Verified from the fork board: P1 pad S1 is at (96.90,-35.20) on net VDD3. Distances from S1 to the nearest VDD3 capacitor pad: C69 43.48 mm, C49 44.57 mm, C5 44.83 mm, then C50 54.0, C34 54.8, C43 64.4, C39 70.9. U18 (TPS22917) sits at (29.474,-27.30) on B.Cu = 67.9 mm. The rail's total derated decoupling is 3 x 1 uF + 4 x 0.1 uF; using my own digitisation of Murata's GRM188R71C105KA12 DC-bias chart (-11.7% at 3.336 V = 0.883 uF) that is 3 x 0.883 + 0.400 = 3.05 uF, against the finding's 3.03 uF. All confirmed. Supporting evidence the finding did not use: insideGadgets' own GBC install instruction is literally 'Device V+ to Capacitor +' - the vendor expects the tap to land on a bypass capacitor, which here it does not. WHY REVISED: the finding explicitly concedes droop is a non-issue (12 mA over a plane pair is nothing - I agree), so the entire case rests on 'there is currently zero local charge reservoir for whatever the module's internal switching does'. That premise is never checked. The ClockxControl is an 18 x 12 x 1.6 mm MCU-plus-oscillator module and will carry its own decoupling on-module, immediately at the die - which is the decoupling that actually matters for its oscillator's jitter. No measurement, no module schematic, no jitter budget is offered. What survives is 'two 0603s of parts already on the BOM are cheap insurance', which is true but is a generic layout principle dressed as a board-specific defect. Downgrade the confidence from 0.75 to roughly 0.35 and file it as optional, not as a reason to respin. Placement caveat also worth tightening: a 0603 centred at (100.5,-37.0) oriented vertically reaches y = -38.5, only 0.45 mm clear of the stated ECO-6 mezzanine window edge at -38.95, so it is tighter than 'clear of' suggests. Benefit is correctly stated as 0 mW.

findings.title: L1/L2 DCR is the only real efficiency lever in this domain - worth 3 mW normally, 6 mW overclocked, 11 mW at max brightness plus overclock
findings.current_part: Taiyo Yuden LSXND3030QKT4R7MNG (previous PN NRS3015T4R7MNGH): 4.7 uH +/-20 %, DCR 0.120 Ohm typ / 0.144 Ohm max, Isat 1.02 A at dL = 30 %, Itemp 1.04 A at dT = 40 C, body 3.0 x 3.0 x 1.5 mm max, terminal e = 0.9 +/-0.2 mm, f = 1.9 +/-0.2 mm. The KiCad footprint is misleadingly named L_Taiyo-Yuden_NR-20xx_HandSoldering but its pads are 1.65 x 2.00 mm on a 2.35 mm pitch, i.e. copper from 0.35 to 1.55 mm from centre - which correctly captures the 3030 part's terminals at 0.6 to 1.5 mm with sensible overhang. So the land is right and only the library name is wrong.
findings.proposal: Wurth WE-MAPI 74438356047: 4.7 uH +/-20 %, DCR 63 mOhm typ / 76 mOhm max, Isat(30 %) 5.75 A typ, IRP,40K 4 A, body 4.1 x 4.1 x 2.1 mm, recommended land 1.39 mm pads on a 3.7 mm span with a 3.35 mm pad height. Only L2 needs it (ch2 carries the CPU/SRAM/logic/audio load and takes all the overclock current); L1 can stay. I checked the obvious same-footprint alternatives and they are all worse: Taiyo Yuden LSDND3030MKT4R7MM (metal composite, 3.0 x 3.0 x 1.2 mm, identical e/f terminals) is 0.228 Ohm typ / 0.263 max, and LCDND3030KKT4R7MM (3.0 x 3.0 x 1.0 mm) is 0.300 typ / 0.345 max. There is no drop-in improvement on the existing land - the fitted part is already the best of the family.
findings.benefit: P = DCR x (I_L1^2 + I_L2^2), using typical DCR. At 792 mW in use (I_L1 = 132 mA, I_L2 = 198 mA): 0.120 x (0.01742 + 0.03920) = 6.8 mW today, 0.063 x same = 3.6 mW with the MAPI, saving 3.2 mW. With the overclock (I_L2 = 299 mA): 0.120 x (0.01742 + 0.08940) = 12.8 mW today vs 6.7 mW, saving 6.1 mW. At the Hispeedido max-brightness point 1175 mW plus overclock (I_L1 = 220 mA, I_L2 = 371 mA): 0.120 x (0.04862 + 0.13727) = 22.3 mW today vs 11.7 mW, saving 10.6 mW. Using max DCR instead of typ the numbers become 8.2/15.4/26.8 mW today, saving up to 12.6 mW. Set against a 792-1420 mW overclocked in-use budget that is 0.4 % to 0.8 % of system power - real, but it will not show up on a battery-life graph. Note the overclock by itself adds 6 mW of inductor loss (12.8 - 6.8) at the 792 mW point purely from the extra 101 mA on L2.
findings.risk: Three separate problems, all real. (1) It does not fit on the current layout: a 4.1 x 4.1 mm body centred on L2 (29.5, -34.8) sweeps a courtyard of roughly x 27.25-31.75, y -37.05 to -32.55, which collides with C42 (30.77-32.73, -39.90 to -36.50); doing the same at L1 (29.5, -45) collides with C21 and grazes U11. Both bulk output caps would have to move. (2) Height goes from 1.5 mm to 2.1 mm on B.Cu, which faces the cart/battery side of a GBA shell - I have no verified clearance figure and this must be measured on a real shell before committing. (3) The 4.7 uH value must be kept: the LTC3527 datasheet says 3.3-4.7 uH suits 1.2 MHz operation and that larger inductance slightly raises maximum output current, and channel 2's headroom is already the thin one (the datasheet's Maximum Output Current vs VIN curve for converter 2 reads roughly 300 mA at VIN = 2.4 V, VOUT = 3.3 V, against my estimated ~150 mA VOUT3 load with the overclock - fine at 2.4 V, less comfortable at the 1.8 V end of discharge). Verdict: real but marginal; I would take the sram and clockxcontrol fixes first and only do this if the board is being respun anyway.
findings.verify_reason: Direction and both part specs are right; the headline savings are inflated ~45% by an internal inconsistency. PARTS VERIFIED: Taiyo Yuden LSXND3030QKT4R7MNG on DigiKey - 4.7 uH +/-20%, DCR max 144 mOhm, Isat 1.02 A, Itemp 1.04 A, 1212 (3030 Metric), 1.50 mm max seated height, semi-shielded, Active. (The 120 mOhm typ figure comes only from the Taiyo Yuden listing, not from a page I could open directly - treat typ as lightly sourced; the 144 mOhm max is solid.) Wurth 74438356047 verified from the Wurth datasheet PDF, exactly as claimed: WE-MAPI 4020, 4.7 uH +/-20%, RDC 63 mOhm typ / 76 mOhm max, ISAT,30% 5.75 A typ, ISAT,10% 3.05 A, IRP,40K 4 A, body 4.1 +/-0.2 x 4.1 +/-0.2 x 2.1 max, recommended land 1.39 mm pads / 3.35 mm pad height / 3.7 mm span. LTC3527 quotes verified verbatim: 'Inductor values between 3.3uH and 4.7uH are suitable for most 1.2MHz applications' and 'Larger values of inductance will allow slightly greater output current capability (and lower the Burst Mode threshold)'. COLLISIONS VERIFIED from the board: C42 is at (31.75,-38.2) rot 90 so its courtyard maps to x 30.77-32.73, y -39.90 to -36.50, and a 4.5 mm courtyard at L2 (29.5,-34.8) spans x 27.25-31.75, y -37.05 to -32.55 - overlapping in both axes. Same for C21 (31.75,-41.6 rot -90 -> x 30.77-32.73, y -43.30 to -39.90) against L1 at (29.5,-45). ARITHMETIC ERROR: the savings apply 63 mOhm to BOTH inductors while the proposal says 'Only L2 needs it; L1 can stay.' Redone with L1 kept at 120 mOhm: at 792 mW (I_L1 132 mA, I_L2 198 mA) loss goes 0.120x0.017424 + 0.063x0.039204 = 4.56 mW against 6.80 mW, SAVING 2.2 mW not 3.2; overclocked (I_L2 299 mA) 7.72 vs 12.82 mW, SAVING 5.1 mW not 6.1; max-brightness-plus-overclock (220/371 mA) 14.48 vs 22.32 mW, SAVING 7.8 mW not 10.6. The finding's numbers are only obtainable by swapping both, which then also forces C21 to move. So the honest headline is 0.28% of system power normally, 0.36% overclocked. TWO SMALLER ERRORS: the land arithmetic is wrong - pads 1.65 x 2.00 at +/-1.175 give copper from 0.35 to 2.00 mm from centre, not 0.35 to 1.55; the conclusion (the land captures the 0.6-1.5 mm terminals) survives and is in fact more generous than stated. And the 'no drop-in improvement exists on this land' claim was tested only inside the Taiyo Yuden 3030 family; other vendors were not searched. I could not confirm a better same-land 4.7 uH part within budget (Coilcraft XGL3020 appears not to reach 4.7 uH), so treat that as unresolved rather than established. The input-current split is also not constant across the finding: 40:60 at the 792 mW point but ~45:55 at the 1175 mW point, undeclared. Verdict on the recommendation itself is unchanged: real, small, respin-only, and behind the SRAM fix.

findings.title: C21 loses 51 % of its capacitance at 5.014 V and is the sole bulk cap on the rail that feeds the backlight - still legal, but it is the tightest node on the board
findings.current_part: C21 = Murata GRM21BR61E226ME44L, 22 uF +/-20 % 25 V X5R 0805, body 2.0 x 1.25 x 1.25 mm, cap change rate +/-15 % over -55 to +85 C. Murata's own DC-bias chart, digitised: -51.5 % at 5.014 V, giving 10.66 uF. Add the tolerance and the X5R temperature band and the worst case is 22 x 0.80 x 0.485 x 0.85 = 7.25 uF. The only other capacitor on VOUT5 is C72, 0.1 uF, which contributes 0.099 uF. So the rail has 10.76 uF effective against 22.1 uF nominal, i.e. 49 %.
findings.proposal: No change required. If you are respinning the board anyway, add a second 22 uF 0805 land in parallel with C21 on B.Cu near U5 pin 5 (VOUT1). Do not try to solve this with a bigger nominal value in the same 0805: I could not obtain a verified DC-bias curve for the obvious candidate (Murata GRM21BR60J476ME15L, 47 uF 6.3 V X5R 0805), and 6.3 V-rated dielectric at a 5.0 V bias is exactly the case where the derating is worst, so substituting it on faith would be a mistake. Marked unverified deliberately.
findings.benefit: No power saving. The reason to know this number: VOUT5 is the rail that carries the LCD analog supply VSHA (FFC pin 34, via U11) and therefore the brightness-dependent load - the 568-to-1175 mW swing on a Hispeedido panel is this rail. It is also the rail with the least bulk capacitance in effective terms (10.8 uF, versus 28.0 uF on VOUT3), and if the screen kit PWM-dims the backlight, VOUT5 sees the resulting load steps. The LTC3527 is specified as stable with COUT >= 4.7 uF and the datasheet recommends 4.7-10 uF with "larger values up to 22 uF" for lower ripple and better transient response, so at 10.7 uF typical and 7.25 uF worst case the rail is compliant with margin - it just has far less margin than the 22 uF marking suggests. Burst-mode ripple, which the datasheet gives as typically 1 % p-p, is also already mitigated by C40, the 15 pF C0G feed-forward cap the datasheet asks for.
findings.risk: None from leaving it alone. Adding a parallel 22 uF costs board area on a crowded B.Cu and would raise the load current at which channel 1 leaves Burst Mode (the datasheet warns that "larger output capacitor values may cause this transition to occur at lighter loads"), which would slightly hurt idle efficiency on the 5 V channel. On balance, leave it.
findings.verify_reason: I did not take the digitised curve on trust - I fetched Murata's own datasheet for GRM21BR61E226ME44L, rendered its DC-bias chart, located the gridlines by pixel analysis (x: 0 V at px 344, 30 V at px 1135; y: 0% at px 33, -100% at px 508) and read the blue trace. At 5.014 V I get -51.7% -> 10.63 uF, against the finding's -51.5% -> 10.66 uF. Match. The same PDF confirms the rest verbatim: 22 uF +/-20%, 25 Vdc, X5R (EIA), capacitance change rate +/-15.0%, -55 to 85 C, L 2.0+/-0.2, W 1.25+/-0.2, T 1.25+/-0.2, size code 2012 (0805). DigiKey confirms the part Active. Worst case recomputed: 22 x 0.80 x 0.483 x 0.85 = 7.22 uF (finding 7.25). With C72 at 0.099 uF the rail carries 10.73 uF effective against 22.1 uF nominal = 48.6% (finding 49%). LTC3527 margins verified verbatim from the datasheet: 'The internal loop compensation ... is designed to be stable with output capacitor values of 4.7uF or greater' and 'A 4.7uF to 10uF output capacitor is sufficient for most applications. Larger values up to 22uF may be used to obtain lower output voltage ripple and improve transient response.' Burst ripple 'typically 1% peak-to-peak' and the 15 pF feedforward recommendation both confirmed. VOUT5 = 1.20 x (1 + 1.78/0.56) = 5.014 V confirmed from the datasheet's 1.20 V reference. The refusal to substitute a 47 uF 6.3 V 0805 on an unverified curve is exactly the right call and is honestly labelled. One trivial nit: DigiKey lists seated height max 1.45 mm, not the 1.25 mm body T. Nothing in the conclusion moves.

findings.title: VDD2 decoupling does NOT need strengthening at the CPU for 7.34 MHz - the numbers say it has an order of magnitude of margin
findings.current_part: Inventory from the net map: C60 10 uF 0603 (25 V X5R) at (18.4, -33.8) on B.Cu, 3.5 mm from U8 - this is the LDO's output capacitor, not CPU decoupling, and it is 33 mm from the CPU. Local to U1: C45/C46/C47/C48 1 uF 16 V X7R and C8/C15/C16/C52/C53 0.1 uF 50 V X7R. After derating at 2.5 V: 7.39 + 4 x 0.968 + 5 x 0.1007 = 11.76 uF total, of which 4.37 uF is local to the CPU. VDD2 is a plane on In2.Cu (zone x 16.8-101.8, y -63.2 to -31.6) over a solid In1.Cu ground plane. NCV8164 requires COUT >= 1 uF ceramic with no minimum ESR, Iq 30 uA typ, dropout 125 mV typ at 300 mA for the 2.5 V variant, current limit 350 mA min.
findings.proposal: Change nothing at U1. Three independent checks all clear comfortably. (1) Target impedance: allow 5 % ripple on 2.5 V = 125 mV; taking my estimated 117 mA of CPU dynamic current at 7.34 MHz and a 50 % step, Ztarget = 0.125/0.058 = 2.15 Ohm. (2) Charge transfer per clock: Q = 0.117 A / 7.34 MHz = 15.9 nC; against the 4.37 uF of local effective capacitance that is dV = 3.6 mV per cycle, 35x under budget. (3) High-frequency impedance: at an estimated 1.5-2.5 nH of mounting-plus-via loop inductance per 0603 (engineering estimate, not a datasheet figure), nine caps in parallel give ~0.22 nH, so |Z| at 200 MHz = 2*pi*2e8*0.22e-9 = 0.28 Ohm, still 7x under the 2.15 Ohm target. The physical placement backs this up: every one of U1's four VDD2 pins has a 0.1 uF within 2.4-3.7 mm and a 1 uF within 2.5-4.5 mm.
findings.benefit: No power saving. The value of this finding is negative-result value: the obvious instinct with a 1.75x overclock is to pile capacitance onto VDD2, and the arithmetic says that would be wasted board area and wasted money. The one place the network genuinely IS weak is the SRAM, which is a separate finding. Worth adding: because U8 is an LDO, every milliamp the overclock adds to VDD2 also comes out of VOUT3 and burns (3.336 - 2.500) = 0.836 V in U8 - 50 mA of extra core current costs 42 mW of pure heat in a SOT-23-5.
